articles.summary: How China and the EU pressed pause on trade war – and what it took to get there  South China Morning PostEU Aims to Put Brakes on Chinese Hybrid-Vehicle Market Share With Import Cap  WSJEU hybrid curbs to offer only ‘temporary’ respite against Chinese carmakers  Financial TimesChina's $7.5 billion EU hybrid boom faces new curbs under China-EU deal  ReutersChinese Lithium Slumps 10% After EU Deal Slashes Hybrid Exports  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
EU officials spoke of a ‘paradigm shift’ in wake of surprise trade deal, saying the ‘nature of the rebalancing exercise has changed’
Weeks of high-wire negotiations between China and the EU culminated in a surprise trade deal that will, among other measures, impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc and slash Chinese tariffs on a variety of European goods.
The deal, unveiled on Friday, takes some of the heat out of searing bilateral trade tensions and temporarily averts the prospect of a bruising trade war.
Beijing agreed not to retaliate against Brussels’ move to curb imports of Chinese hybrid cars, which will see shipments capped at 350,000 units per year, rising at 6 per cent annually. This will leave exports at less than half the 800,000 vehicles the EU has projected will be shipped in 2026.
Asked on Monday how Beijing grew to accept the concessions – after Chinese officials spent weeks rejecting the prospect of voluntarily limiting auto shipments – Brussels framed its position with a time-worn business maxim: “The customer is always right.”

articles.title: Pakistani Industry Opposes Rs 268 Billion Power Tariff Burden - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Pakistani Industry Opposes Rs 268 Billion Power Tariff Burden  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Pakistan's industrial sector is mounting fierce resistance against a proposed Rs 268 billion power tariff adjustment, warning that the additional financial burden threatens to stifle manufacturing competitiveness and derail ongoing export recovery efforts.
The Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry has formally appealed to the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority and the federal government to reject the tariff hike. Business leaders argue that for Pakistani textiles and heavy industries to survive regionally, industrial electricity rates must be reduced below nine US cents per unit, a threshold that current adjustment proposals fail to address.
The Rs 268 Billion Adjustment Dispute
The controversy centers on a massive revenue requirement that power distribution companies have submitted to the regulator for the second quarter and full calendar year of 2026. The proposed adjustments, amounting to Rs 268 billion, are designed to cover shortfalls in fuel costs, capacity payments to independent power producers, and grid losses. However, the business community views these adjustments as a structural penalty on productive sectors of the economy, effectively forcing industries to subsidize the inefficiencies of the national grid and the government's delayed subsidy disbursements.
The Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry has organized press conferences and submitted detailed briefs to the Ministry of Energy, arguing that continuous quarterly tariff notifications create an unpredictable operating environment. Industrialists contend that the cumulative effect of these adjustments has pushed the cost of doing business to unsustainable levels, leading to factory closures and a shift toward captive power generation, which further reduces the revenue base for the national grid and triggers a vicious cycle of tariff hikes.
The Nine-Cent Competitiveness Threshold
At the heart of the industry's counter-proposal is a demand for a fixed, regionally competitive energy rate. The federation has consistently called for an industrial power tariff below nine US cents per unit, a benchmark they argue is necessary to compete with manufacturing hubs in Bangladesh and Vietnam. Current effective rates, which frequently exceed twelve to fifteen cents per unit when factoring in fuel price adjustments and surcharges, render Pakistani exports uncompetitive in global markets.
The business body has warned that proposed tariff schemes offering only temporary or marginal relief are insufficient to address the underlying competitiveness gap. By focusing on short-term revenue recovery rather than structural cost reduction, regulators risk accelerating the deindustrialization of the economy. The chamber has urged the government to absorb the Rs 268 billion burden through targeted fiscal measures or debt restructuring, rather than passing the cost directly onto the commercial and industrial consumers who drive the country's foreign exchange earnings.
Regulatory Proceedings and Grid Economics
The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority is currently reviewing the petitions submitted by the distribution companies, holding public hearings that have become battlegrounds between consumer protection advocates and power sector financiers. The regulator faces the difficult task of balancing the financial viability of the power sector against the broader macroeconomic stability of the country. If the full Rs 268 billion adjustment is approved, it will trigger an immediate spike in monthly electricity bills, likely fueling inflation and dampening consumer demand across the retail sector.
Grid economics in Pakistan are heavily skewed by a massive circular debt crisis, where the government struggles to pay power generators due to unrecovered bills and systemic theft. The regulatory framework mandates that these shortfalls be passed on to consumers through quarterly adjustments, a mechanism that the business community argues is fundamentally flawed. Industry representatives have suggested that without a comprehensive overhaul of the transmission network and a strict crackdown on non-payment, tariff adjustments will remain a permanent fixture of the national budget.
Export Survival and Structural Reforms
The standoff over the Rs 268 billion adjustment is ultimately a battle for the survival of Pakistan's export-oriented industries. The textile sector, which accounts for the lion's share of national exports, operates on thin margins and is highly sensitive to energy costs. Prolonged exposure to double-digit cent tariffs has already forced several major manufacturers to scale back operations or relocate production facilities to special economic zones that offer subsidized energy rates, leaving the broader industrial base vulnerable.
As the federal government negotiates with international financial institutions, the energy sector remains a primary focal point for structural reforms. The business community is demanding that future loan conditions prioritize industrial competitiveness over immediate revenue generation, arguing that a thriving export sector is the only sustainable path to resolving the circular debt crisis. Until the structural inefficiencies of the power sector are addressed, the friction between regulators seeking cost recovery and industries fighting for survival will continue to define Pakistan's economic landscape.

articles.title: Germany's Wadephul calls new EU sanctions 'unprecedented' blow to Russia - DW.com
articles.summary: Germany's Wadephul calls new EU sanctions 'unprecedented' blow to Russia  DW.comEU sanctions nearly 1,600 Russian people and firms linked to drone and missile parts  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosEurope pushes tougher line on Russia in growing split with Trump  POLITICO.euRussia’s war of aggression against Ukraine: EU agrees largest-ever package of listings targeting almost 1600 individuals and entities in Russia’s military-industrial complex ...
articles.full_text:
German foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described a new raft of punitive measures against Russia as an "unprecedented sanction blow" to President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.
"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said on Monday as EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.
Who do the sanctions target?
It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that this was "the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war...More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
"We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she added.
Although he could not attend the Luxembourg meeting due to a party conference in Berlin, Wadephul said: "The message is clear: Russia cannot and will not win this war."
However, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to imply that sanctions need to go even further as the conflict was set to enter its fifth bitter winter.
"This is the moment when the entire West...should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, referring to EU sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia.
What is the latest development in the war?
Russian forces have repeatedly stepped up attacks on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure every autumn since its invasion, hoping to cripple heating and other necessary utilitiesahead of winter.
US President Donald Trump declared that there was an "energy ceasefire" in place between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had no idea what Trump was referring to and that Russia had continued to target energy facilities unabated.

articles.title: Japanese FDI capital is driving green transformation in Vietnamese industrial production. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Japanese FDI capital is driving green transformation in Vietnamese industrial production.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In particular, investments from FDI capital flows reflect the long-term vision and confidence of Japanese businesses in the potential for sustainable economic growth in Vietnam and the region.
Highlights of investment cooperation
In fact, a bright spot in Vietnam-Japan economic relations has been investment cooperation, a prime example over the past several years. According to statistics from the Trade Promotion Agency of the Ministry of Industry and Trade , Japan has over 5,800 active projects in Vietnam with a total investment capital exceeding US$81 billion. Simultaneously, numerous Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) continue to facilitate businesses in both countries in terms of tariffs, rules of origin, and trade facilitation, expanding opportunities for deeper participation in regional supply chains and production networks.
In particular, a number of Japanese corporations and businesses are not only committed to but also continuously expanding their production in Vietnam, such as Honda, Panasonic, Kao Vietnam, Sumitomo, etc. Meanwhile, a new wave of investment from Japanese businesses is continuously flowing into Vietnamese industrial parks, contributing to promoting green transformation in production in line with sustainable development trends, with solutions that meet market demands and can adapt to new requirements.
For example, OJI Group, Japan, recently commenced construction of a new aseptic carton packaging plant in Vietnam under the Oji Liquid Pak (OLP) brand, with a total investment of US$110 million, at the Long Thanh High-Tech Park, Dong Nai province. The project demonstrates Oji Liquid Pak's long-term investment commitment in Vietnam, while also affirming Vietnam's strategic role as a manufacturing and supply hub in the Group's growth strategy in Southeast Asia, contributing to the region's shift towards circular packaging solutions and meeting policy requirements.
Mr. Nguyen Quoc An, Deputy Head of the Management Board of Industrial Parks and Economic Zones of Dong Nai City (DNIEZA), stated that large-scale projects like these not only contribute to promoting the development of the local industry but also create opportunities to enhance domestic production capacity and strengthen Vietnam's participation in the regional supply chain. The Management Board of Industrial Parks and Economic Zones of Dong Nai City commits to continuing to support and facilitate investors throughout the project implementation process, within its assigned functions, duties, and authority; promptly guiding and coordinating the resolution of any difficulties and obstacles that arise so that the project is implemented in accordance with regulations and can commence operations as soon as possible.
Mr. Kestutis Sliuzas, General Director of Oji Liquid Pak, shared that more and more manufacturing industries, including the packaging industry, are shifting to a new standard where efficiency, food safety, operational flexibility, and circular economy elements must go hand in hand. Therefore, the Oji Liquid Pak Co., Ltd. factory project combines the production of packaging for the food industry with research and development, technical services, installation, and maintenance of Japanese-made machinery, thereby contributing to the goal of creating a modern, high-quality, and high-value-added production environment in the industrial park.
You may also like
According to some experts, besides manufacturing, Japanese FDI flows into diverse fields such as research and development in natural sciences; repair, maintenance, and installation of machinery and equipment; and import, export, and distribution of goods in accordance with Vietnamese law . These are areas that have a positive impact on the development orientation of Vietnamese industrial parks in the current period.
Mr. Tran Viet Ha, Deputy Head of the Ho Chi Minh City Export Processing Zones and Industrial Parks Management Board (HEPZA), stated that facilitating investors' early project implementation after registration and reducing procedures related to planning and construction are the goals that HEPZA is focusing on currently and in the near future. Specifically, HEPZA will directly handle issues within its jurisdiction, while inter-agency matters will be handled in coordination; simultaneously, the approach will shift from a centralized administrative procedure to continuous monitoring and management throughout the project implementation process, from investment preparation to operation.
On the other hand, Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy also sets out an important policy direction, shifting the strategic focus of Vietnam's investment attraction from prioritizing the quantity of foreign investment to emphasizing quality, specifically investments that bring high technology, innovation, human resource development, and technology transfer. Vietnam is no longer a destination for simple assembly activities based on cheap labor, but is positioning itself as a center for high value-added, technology-based investment.
Corporate responsibility
Entering a new era, with a strong shift from attracting investment based on quantity to attracting selective investment, many industrial parks in localities such as Ho Chi Minh City, Dong Nai, etc., are prioritizing projects with advanced technology, high added value, efficient land use, environmental friendliness, and the ability to participate in and enhance the locality's position in domestic and global supply chains. In this orientation, many industrial parks also demonstrate a particularly important role in creating space to accommodate projects with high quality, advanced technology and management methods, especially those demonstrating corporate responsibility towards the environment and the community.
Regarding the Japanese business community in Vietnam, Mr. ONO Masuo, Consul General of Japan in Ho Chi Minh City, assessed that, along with production, the community contributions of Japanese businesses over the years have further deepened the relationship between Japan and Vietnam. A prime example is Kao Vietnam, a Japanese company, which has strived to improve hygiene, protect health, and enhance the quality of life in Vietnam through programs such as the "Kao Hygiene Development Program in Vietnam," implemented since 2018, in addition to its production and business activities.
Recently, Kao Vietnam Company initiated the "Healthcare Enhancement Program: Improving the Health of Female Workers in Industrial Zones." This program, implemented by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in collaboration with the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women), government agencies, healthcare units, and workplace stakeholders, demonstrates Japanese businesses' proactive contribution to the local community and their role in addressing social issues in Vietnam.
Mr. ONO Masuo further informed that the Vietnamese government has set clear economic growth targets towards 2030, and the process of improving institutions and infrastructure is progressing steadily. In addition, the living conditions and working environment of the people are constantly changing, especially in ensuring the legitimate rights of workers.
You may also like
On the business side, Mr. Shintaro Yasue, General Director of Kao Vietnam, said that the company started operating in Vietnam in 1996 and 2026 marks Kao's 30th anniversary in this market. Throughout the past three decades, the company has continuously developed its production and business sustainably, adapting to the changes in Vietnamese society and people's lives.
Entering the next phase of its development, Kao Vietnam aims to continue delivering new value to consumers, not only through strengthening its brand and products, but also by promoting initiatives that contribute to solving social problems in Vietnam. This is also part of the company's long-term and sustainable development strategy, with a desire to find ways to enhance corporate responsibility and contribute more to the local community.
Particularly in a rapidly developing urban area like Ho Chi Minh City, a large number of women actively participate in the workforce and social activities. Therefore, by applying their experience, the manufacturing business community can develop diverse initiatives that contribute to improving the health and lives of working women in Vietnam, helping female workers feel secure and work effectively.

articles.title: Malaysia yet to receive US signal on semiconductor tariffs, says Johari - NST Online
articles.summary: Malaysia yet to receive US signal on semiconductor tariffs, says Johari  NST Online
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia has yet to receive any indication that the United States (US) plans to impose tariffs on its semiconductor exports, Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said.
He said the government had not received any notification from Washington suggesting that Malaysian semiconductor products would be subject to tariffs.
"At this point, there is no indication that the US will impose any tariffs on semiconductors from Malaysia," he told reporters at a press conference during EU-Malaysia Business Day 2026: Selangor in Focus here today.
Johari was responding to a question on whether Malaysian semiconductor products would continue to be exempt from US tariffs.
He had also previously said that Malaysia was seeking to diversify its electrical and electronics (E&E) value chain, broaden its economic growth drivers and expand export markets to reduce its vulnerability to downturns in the global semiconductor cycle.
What To Read Next
Under the New Industrial Master Plan (NIMP) 2030 and National Semiconductor Strategy (NSS), the government is focusing on higher value-added, technology-intensive activities such as integrated circuit design and advanced packaging.
Commenting on Malaysia's trade negotiations with Washington, Johari said discussions under Section 301 covered four main areas, namely forced labour, excess production capacity, environmental standards and government subsidies.
He said Malaysia was in a favourable position on environmental compliance and government subsidies, noting that the country did not subsidise companies specifically to support exports to overseas markets.
"On the environmental front, we are in a good position as we safeguard the environment and comply with the requirements set by developed economies.
"On government subsidies, our position is clear because we do not provide subsidies to companies to export to other countries," he said.
Johari said the forced labour issue had also been resolved, with Malaysia subject to a 10 per cent rate, compared with 12.5 per cent for some other economies, as outlined in his explanation of the negotiations.
However, he said excess production capacity remained an outstanding issue, although Malaysia maintained that it did not have a domestic overcapacity problem.
He said any excess capacity associated with goods exported from Malaysia could originate from third countries rather than local production.
He maintained that Malaysia had no domestic overcapacity, adding that any excess capacity linked to exports from the country would originate from third countries rather than local production.
Johari also said Malaysia wanted the US to identify the countries it believed were responsible for excess capacity so that appropriate action could be taken.
He noted that countries had their own laws and requirements governing access to their domestic markets, which exporters must meet to maintain access to international trade.
He said Malaysian exporters must comply with each country's regulations and market-entry requirements to gain access to its market.

articles.title: Tariff-ied! This Week in International Trade (October 12, 2026) - The National Law Review
articles.summary: Tariff-ied! This Week in International Trade (October 12, 2026)  The National Law Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaway: In today’s tariff-heavy enforcement environment, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is not waiting for problems to reveal themselves. It is increasingly using data mining and other analytics to identify classification, valuation, origin, and other trade-data anomalies, resulting in sharply increased use of CF-28 Requests for Information as a result. These inquiries should not be treated as routine or being limited to the single entry under review, as CBP expects importers to apply the result of any determination across all analogous entries. A CF-28 often is a warning that CBP is looking at an entire pattern or type of imports, and importers that fail to respond accordingly risk inviting broader scrutiny, additional duty exposure, and potential enforcement consequences.
This Week in International Trade: Does CBP really have a DEFCON-style tracking center? Well, if NORAD tracks Santa every Christmas Eve, why not? Maybe they even share tracking equipment.
This week’s international trade developments include the following:
Tariff Refunds
| • | CAPE refund processing continues at scale. As of October 2nd, CBP had received 297,887 Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (CAPE) declarations. 209,262 passed validation, covering 27.4 million entries representing about $136.6 billion in potential and certified refunds accepted for processing. 6.2 million entries failed validation, primarily because they were outside CBP’s 90-day reliquidation window, lacked the Chapter 99 HTS numbers tied to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) duties, or had already been submitted on a prior declaration. | 
| • | CBP deploys CAPE Phase 3 for finally liquidated entries under court order. CBP successfully launched Phase 3 of the CAPE refund system on October 6 for finally liquidated entries belonging to importers that sued in the Court of International Trade (CIT) and obtained court-ordered reliquidation that had provided their importer of record information by July 31, 2026. 477 declarations covering 425,517 entries have been accepted. CBP has indicated that it will soon issue instructions for other importers who provided their Importer of Record (IOR) information later than July 31st. | 
Tariff Litigation
| • | IEEPA refund dispute continues over AD/CVD ‘type three’ entries. Judge Eaton is moving towards a resolution of how CBP should treat entries subject to both IEEPA duties and antidumping/countervailing duties (AD/CVD). Judge Eaton directed plaintiffs and plaintiff-intervenor the National Seafood Association to file refund-related motions by October 19th, with the government’s response due November 9th. AD/CVD entries are the largest remaining class of entries with no refund mechanism. The issue is how such refunds would occur, when AD/CVD duties can take years to reach a final and definitive duty rate. | 
| • | CIT certifies nationwide importer class in IEEPA refund litigation. The CIT certified a nationwide Rule 23(b)(2) class in the lead IEEPA refund case, opening a path for non-litigating importers, who may not have enough at stake to warrant a CIT 1581(i) filing, to gain refunds. The ruling is intended to broaden access to refunds for importers left out of CAPE or deterred by litigation cost, but a Department of Justice (DOJ) appeal is expected. Right now, filing a 1581(i) action remains the surest and quickest way to get a refund of finally liquidated entries. | 
| • | Section 122 tariff litigation stayed pending appeal. The Court of International Trade stayed multiple pending challenges to the Section 122 tariffs until the Federal Circuit resolves the appeals from the CIT’s May 2026 ruling that President Trump unlawfully invoked Section 122. For importers, the validity and collection of these tariffs will remain uncertain until the appellate process is completed, including potential Supreme Court review. | 
Tariff Policy
| • | USTR continues the Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods. In a development that surprised exactly no one, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has kept the Section 301 tariffs on China, first imposed in the Trump administration, in place. | 
| • | USTR opens consultation ahead of 2027 USMCA joint review. USTR launched a public consultation process ahead of the 2027 United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) joint review, requesting comments by January 12, 2027, on implementation, compliance, competitiveness, investment, economic security, and responses to non-market practices. Because the United States previously declined to confirm continuation of the agreement, annual joint reviews will now occur until all parties agree to extend the agreement or termination occurs in 2036. | 
| • | Commerce clarifies U.S.-content rules for modified metal tariffs on Canadian and Mexican goods. Commerce issued guidance on how CBP will determine the U.S.-content portion of certain Canadian and Mexican steel, aluminum, and copper products for purposes of Trump’s modified tariff regimes, under which USMCA-qualifying goods are subject to the 25% duty only on their non-U.S. content. The clarification gives importers a clearer allocation methodology but heightens the importance of origin tracing, value support, and supply-chain documentation. | 
| • | Milwaukee Framework signals new global management of steel overcapacity. The United States and 27 other members of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity adopted the “Milwaukee Framework,” a coordinated trade-enforcement initiative aimed at addressing global steel overcapacity associated largely with China, including potential self-initiated AD/CVD cases, enhanced supply-chain monitoring, and stronger circumvention and evasion oversight. The framework suggests greater enforcement pressure on steel sourcing and customs compliance, even if future tariff measures remain uncertain. | 
Import Regulations & Enforcement
| • | CBP proposes major overhaul of low-value import procedures. CBP proposed significant changes for shipments valued at $2,500 or less, including mandatory electronic filing for informal and mail entries, creation of a new electronic mail entry type, bond requirements for all such entries, broker requirements for non-owner consignees, additional shipper and tracking data elements, abandonment rules for unentered mail, and liquidated damages exposure for bond defaults. The proposal would also allow certain Chapter 99 goods valued between $250 and $2,500 to use informal entry procedures. | 
| • | DOJ elevates trade fraud as a core enforcement priority. DOJ’s Fraud Division has made trade-related fraud – including tariff evasion, import fraud, and forced-labor-related misconduct – a core enforcement priority, instructing prosecutors to weigh aggravating factors such as long-running schemes, large losses, concealment, management involvement, and threats to U.S. security. Expanded whistleblower initiatives and centralized corporate enforcement oversight signal increased scrutiny of import compliance programs and higher enforcement risk for import operations. | 
| • | DOJ seeks major penalties in tile importer customs evasion case. DOJ filed a significant customs fraud action in the Court of International Trade against a tile importer and its CEO, alleging they evaded $67.9 million in AD/CVD on Chinese goods through transshipment via Malaysia, undervaluation, misdescription, and use of shell companies after a CBP Enforce and Protect Act (EAPA) investigation began. The government is seeking $222.5 million in civil penalties under 19 U.S.C. § 1592 in addition to unpaid duties. | 
| • | EAPA interim measures face renewed due-process challenge. Three more golf-cart and low-speed vehicle importers asked the CIT to block CBP interim measures imposed in an EAPA investigation, arguing that waiting for a final evasion determination would be manifestly inadequate because the interim measures are already causing drastic harm. The government maintains that review must await a final determination under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(c), while the importers rely on the Icon electric vehicle case to support immediate constitutional review. | 
Export Controls & Economic Sanctions Regulations & Enforcement
| • | State Department proposes targeted easing of defense export controls. The State Department proposed revising the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) and U.S. Munitions List to remove certain less-sensitive or catch-all controlled items, create a new license exemption for temporary exports of foreign defense articles back to their foreign manufacturers. Comments are due by November 30th. | 
International Financial Regulations & Enforcement
| • | Large AML penalty underscores trade-based money laundering risk. A large financial institution was fined $350 million over alleged systemic AML deficiencies, including an alleged failure to properly detect and report about $13 billion in suspected trade-based money laundering activity from 2014 to 2025. The case reinforces regulators’ continued focus on having appropriate internal controls, transaction monitoring, customer due diligence, and suspicious activity reporting in cross-border payment and trade-related activity. | 
Cross-Border Transactions
| • | CFIUS data show short-form declarations increasingly end without clearance. New CFIUS data show that short-form declarations are becoming less likely to result in definitive clearance: in 2025, 47 of 140 declarations (about 34%) did not produce clearance, including 36 requests for full notices and 11 “shoulder shrug” outcomes without safe harbor, up from 24 of 116 declarations (about 21%) the year before. This means that foreign investors increasingly need to consider filing full joint voluntary notices which, although taking longer, result in a definitive determination as to whether the transaction has received safe harbor clearance. |

Good afternoon.
I begin today by acknowledging the traditional owners of the land on which we meet and pay my respects to Elders past and present.
My thanks to Innes, John and the Australian Industry Group for the invitation to speak today.
AiG has long been a strong voice for Australian industry.
Your members are the businesses that manufacture, innovate, invest and export.
They create jobs, send our goods to the world, develop new technologies, and help drive Australia's prosperity and global influence.
I have recently returned from the G20 Trade Ministers Meeting in Milwaukee.
Where twenty Trade Ministers from the world's largest economies met to address a range of trade and economic challenges, against backdrop of growing global tensions and protectionism.
I'm sure you can imagine there were some very frank discussions.
The global trading environment is increasingly complex.
Supply chains remain under pressure. Strategic competition is increasing. And economic security is a central concern for governments and businesses alike.
But one message was clear.
The countries that will succeed are not those that close themselves off from the world or subvert the global rules of trade.
They are those that build strong partnerships, diversify their markets and remain active participants in the global economy.
For Australia, trade security does not mean less trade.
It means more diversified trade.
Because trade creates jobs, attracts investment, drives productivity and strengthens economic resilience.
That means more markets, more customers and more opportunities for Australian businesses.
That is why the Albanese Government remains firmly committed to free and fair trade.
Australian businesses and exporters have enormous advantage es.
We produce world-class exports. We are leaders in mining services and resources technology.
And we are building globally competitive capabilities in clean energy, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, defence industries and critical technologies.
Our job as a government is to help Australian businesses take those capabilities to the world.
That starts with opening doors.
Australia's network of free trade agreements now spans almost 90% of the globe, and they give our businesses better access to many of the world's fastest-growing, and most valuable markets.
These agreements reduce barriers, lower costs and provide greater certainty for exporters and investors.
But agreements themselves do not create exports. Australian workers, businesses and investors do.
That is why I encourage Australian companies to fully utilise the opportunities available through Australia's large network of trade agreements.
Of course, Government also has a role to play.
We are helping Australian exporters to identify new opportunities, build capability and diversify their markets through our $55 million Accessing New Markets Initiative.
Through trade missions, market intelligence, business matching and unparalleled in-market expertise, the Government is helping Australian businesses expand into new markets and grow in existing ones.
At the centre of this work is the Trade Diversification Network.
The Network brings together more than 40 peak industry organisations, including the Australian Industry Group, to make sure support is tailored to real business needs.
It is government and industry working together to identify opportunities, remove barriers and deliver practical support.
And it is working. Really working.
In less than a year, the Accessing New Markets Initiative has helped more than 900 exporters generate over $100 million in export sales.
These are important results, and speak to the hard work of exporters, alongside support from Government through agencies like Austrade.
The work that Austrade does in driving these results are critical, which is why I also want to acknowledge the release of Austrade's latest Trade and Investment Report today.
Last year, Austrade supported Australian businesses to achieve over 2,400 trade outcomes worth $8.8 billion.
That exceeded its annual target by more than twofold.
These results were delivered across sectors critical to Australia's future:
Agrifood and consumer products generated $2.2 billion in outcomes.
Defence industries - $2 billion.
And the green economy - $1.7 billion.
We are also seeing the benefits of the Government's trade diversification strategy.
Last year, Southeast Asia delivered Austrade's highest number of trade outcomes, worth $1.6 billion.
Our trade with India has grown significantly, with exports reaching $10 billion in 2025.
And while China remains our largest trading partner, Australian businesses are increasingly finding success across a broader range of markets.
That diversification makes Australia stronger, smarter, more resilient, and secure.
The report also highlights the importance of international investment.
Investment brings much more than capital.
It brings technology, expertise, research partnerships and supply-chain connections.
Over the past decade, international investment has supported nearly 400,000 Australian jobs.
Last financial year, Austrade facilitated 115 investment projects worth a record $15.4 billion.
These projects are expected to create or support more than 19,000 Australian jobs.
And since 2022, Australia's total two way trade has grown from $1.07 trillion to $1.37 trillion, increasing by more than $300 billion.
Together, these results show the enormous contribution trade and investment are making to build the industries, capabilities and jobs Australia will rely on for decades to come.
It is clear that no government cannot rest on its laurels, hoping more trade and opportunity will come our way.
I see my job as pushing more Australian companies out the door.
I am more ambitious for Australian companies than they are for themselves.
That is why concluding negotiations on our newest trade agreement with the European Union earlier this year was such an important achievement.
The European Union is a market of around 450 million consumers and an economy worth almost $33 trillion.
This is not just another trade agreement. Rather it should be viewed as 27 trade agreements, with the 27 countries that make up the EU.
It is twenty-seven massive new opportunities. Twenty-seven new open doors for Australian businesses that have effectively been closed for decades.
And twenty-seven lucrative reasons for business and industry to back this deal.
When the agreement enters into force, 97.8 per cent of Australia's goods exports to the EU will enter duty free.
That means better opportunities for Australian manufacturers, farmers, fishers and foresters, technology firms, service providers and clean energy industries in one of the world's largest markets.
It means lower costs, stronger competitiveness and greater certainty for exporters.
It will also support stronger two-way investment flows, giving businesses greater confidence to invest, expand and create jobs.
Unfortunately, there are those in this very building who want to the throw that out the window.
Right now there is a group agitating against the enormous opportunity this deal represents, and to dump Australia into the basket of countries pursuing a race to the bottom of tariffs and protectionism.
They want to say no to billions of dollars of new trade, and hundreds of millions of new consumers for your businesses.
They're acting against the interests of the millions of Australians they claim to represent…
Farmers on the Riverina who will see significant market access increases for their produce…
The miners who are right now producing the critical minerals that will power the global economy…
And the regional communities who rely on trade for economic opportunity and prosperity…
This group will make doing business harder, as your competitors move in for opportunities they seek to lock you out of.
Decades of prosperity. Decades of bipartisan support for trade.
Abandoned on the whim of a movement experiencing a political identity crisis.
Let me make this clear.
There is no second chance with the EU if we choose to walk away from this deal.
Now is the time for a unified, Australia-first approach to free trade, not for dragging us back decades down the path of protectionism and isolation.
Now is not the time to hamstring the operations of businesses in this room - limiting your opportunities to expand and risking your existing customer bases.
All on the fairytale promise of an Australian economy that simply cannot exist except for in the imagination of politicians selling an empty promise.
They'll use the straw man of action on climate and energy to justify their position.
But make no mistake, they are taking this position based on false ideas about trade.
Protectionism has consequences.
We have seen that around the world - tit for tat measures as countries ratchet up pressure, resulting in higher prices for consumers and less opportunity for exporters.
Angus Taylor knew this when highlighted the benefits of free trade in his maiden speech.
Tony Abbott knew this when his government pursued an aggressive free trade agenda
And Nationals leaders of the past knew this when they fiercely guarded the trade portfolio, recognising the significant benefits of free trade to Aussie farmers.
There is no room for negotiation here, the deal is done.
There is a simple choice before the parliament, accept or reject.
This deal won't pass the parliament on its own.
So today, I implore you to stand up for your members and businesses and demand the members of this parliament see deal through the parliament in the coming months.
Friends, Australia's prosperity has always depended on our ability to engage confidently with the world.
We have always been a great trading nation.
And the lesson from today's global environment is not that we should trade less.
In uncertain times, Australia's answer should not be to retreat.
It should be to compete.
To diversify.
To invest and to attract investment.

articles.summary: IMF says AI investment is giving Thailand’s technology supply chain a boost  Thailand Business News
articles.full_text:
According to IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, the global surge in artificial intelligence investments is helping maintain economic growth around 3%, even amid an energy supply shock. She made these remarks in Bangkok on Monday as the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings kicked off.
She said AI infrastructure spending is generating a substantial demand and investment boost for Asian that manufacture the hardware underpinning the technology, including Thailand. The IMF estimates that the AI boom could add 0.5 to 1 percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies and 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asian economies.
Key points
- The IMF says AI infrastructure investment is helping sustain global growth at approximately 3% in 2026.
- AI investment could add 0.2–0.8 percentage point to growth in emerging Asian economies, including economies involved in hardware supply chains.
- The IMF estimates that AI could eventually augment, downgrade or eliminate 40% of jobs, creating significant implications for employment, skills and productivity.
The remarks come as Thailand seeks to attract more investment into semiconductors, advanced electronics, data centres and other technology-related industries. Strong demand for AI computing infrastructure supports manufacturers and suppliers across Asia, creating opportunities for Thailand to expand its role in regional production networks. The benefits, however, depend on whether investment translates into new productive capacity, stronger exports and higher-value domestic employment.
The IMF also warned that AI’s consequences will extend well beyond investment and trade. Georgieva described the technology as a transformative force affecting employment, education, economic growth and government tax revenues. As businesses automate tasks and shift spending from labour towards capital, some jobs will change or disappear even as new opportunities emerge. Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam highlighted the risk that AI could reduce entry-level employment opportunities for graduates, while World Bank President Ajay Banga pointed to the potential of smaller-scale AI applications in agriculture, education and healthcare.
For Thailand, this creates a two-part policy challenge. The country needs to capture the immediate benefits of AI-related exports and foreign investment while increasing technology adoption among domestic businesses. Without better digital infrastructure, skills development and access to affordable tools, the gains could remain concentrated among large exporters while SMEs and traditional industries struggle to improve productivity. Thailand’s current flood crisis further reinforces the importance of using technology to strengthen logistics, financial services and agricultural resilience.
The IMF is scheduled to release an updated global economic outlook on Tuesday, October 13. Its assessment will help clarify how the institution weighs the benefits of AI investment against energy disruption, geopolitical uncertainty and financial-market risks.
Thailand : Thailand Business News — Economics Coverage
Why it matters: AI offers Thailand a potential growth engine at a time when domestic demand and productivity remain constrained. The challenge is to convert the global investment boom into broad-based gains rather than relying solely on exports of technology-related goods. Skills, infrastructure and wider adoption by Thai businesses will determine how much lasting value the country captures.

articles.title: Section 301 exclusions expire November 2026 - Thomson Reuters tax
articles.summary: Section 301 exclusions expire November 2026  Thomson Reuters tax
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Three U.S. measures expire November 9 and 10, two months before the broader trade truce ends in January.
- The 30-for-30 framework isn’t operative yet, and sub-line exclusions mean relief must be checked line by line.
- The 178 remaining Section 301 exclusions expire November 10 unless USTR extends them, and no extension has been announced.
On September 27 and 28, the White House, the U.S. Trade Representative, and China’s Ministry of Commerce published reciprocal tariff-relief lists as part of a new “30-for-30” framework, the first deliverable from the U.S.-China Board of Trade that Presidents Trump and Xi chartered at their May 2026 Beijing summit. Following Xi’s state visit in late September, Treasury announced a two-month extension of the broader tariff truce, originally struck in Busan in October 2025 and set to expire November 10, 2026, pushing the new deadline to January 10, 2027. As of this writing, that extension hasn’t been formally documented through an executive order or Federal Register notice.
That’s the headline. Here’s what it leaves out: three separate U.S. measures lapse on November 9 and 10, 2026, two months before the truce even ends, and nothing on the record extends them.
If your team is planning against the press release instead of the Federal Register, you’re already behind.
Jump to ↓
What the 30-for-30 framework actually does
|  |  | 
What the 30-for-30 framework actually does
Start with what it isn’t. The $30 billion figure is trade value, calculated against 2024 bilateral trade. It is not a purchase commitment and not an estimate of tariff savings. And as of this writing, none of it is operative. Both governments’ terms condition relief on “respective domestic laws and processes,” and the U.S. side hasn’t issued a Federal Register notice, a proclamation, or an HTSUS Chapter 99 amendment to make any of it claimable.
When it does take effect, the mechanics are precise rather than sweeping. The U.S. list covers 77 tariff lines at the 8-digit HTSUS level: household textiles, small appliances, juvenile products, toys, and similar categories. China’s list covers 1,619 lines, weighted toward agriculture, timber, and fish. Both sides carved out the sectors that matter most: semiconductors, EVs, batteries, rare earths, aircraft, steel, pharmaceuticals, crude, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) are excluded entirely. Even within a covered category, the exclusions run below the tariff-line level. A toy classified under HTSUS 9503.00.00 qualifies, unless it has Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or an Ethernet connection built in.
This is the part that a press release can’t capture and a spreadsheet struggles to track: line-by-line, sub-line exceptions layered on top of a tariff stack that already has four separate legal bases running underneath it. It’s the same headline-versus-reality gap trade teams are running into with tariffs on other countries, too.
How multiple tariffs combine into a 37.5% effective rate on Chinese goods
Today’s effective rate on Chinese goods, roughly 37.5% on most products, isn’t one policy. It’s the sum of a most-favored-nation baseline, a 12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariff, possible legacy Section 301 duties from Lists 1 through 4A (which range from 7.5% to 100%), and Section 232 duties where applicable. Getting there took a Supreme Court ruling that invalidated IEEPA tariffs in February, a terminated executive order, a 150-day Section 122 bridge tariff, and a new forced-labor action that took effect the same day the bridge expired, all inside eight months.
Now overlay the 30-for-30 relief on top of that stack. The Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China (MOFCOM) says more than 90% of covered products will eventually receive most-favored-nation treatment, which on the U.S. side implies waiving the applicable Section 301 layers. But no U.S. instrument yet states the mechanism, and the relief has to be checked against every layer, at the 8- and 10-digit level, for every affected line, not assumed at the summary rate.
This is precisely the kind of complexity that outgrows manual review. Tariff data is drawn from ONESOURCE Global Trade Content: over 155 million regulatory updates a year across more than 220 countries and territories, with an average update time under one business day. When a tariff line’s status can change with a single Federal Register notice, that update speed is the difference between an accurate landed cost and a costly guess. This is increasingly how global trade professionals are approaching the problem. They’re building the habit of keeping tariff, duty, and export control data current directly into their own systems rather than checking it separately.
When do the Section 301 exclusions expire?
The 178 remaining Section 301 China exclusions expire on November 10, 2026. Entries filed on or after that date lose the exclusion and are assessed at the standard Section 301 rate for their tariff line, unless USTR issues another extension before then. As of this writing, no extension has been announced.
Your trade compliance calendar: The November-to-January deadline map
Here’s the mismatch in one view. The political calendar says the truce runs to January 10, 2027. The regulatory calendar says three separate measures resolve on November 9 and 10, 2026, two months earlier, with nothing extending them on the record:
| Date | Measure | Status after the date | What to do | 
|---|---|---|---|
| November 9, 2026 | BIS Affiliates Rule suspension ends | Rule reinstates automatically, worldwide | Review affiliate screening obligations | 
| November 9, 2026 | Section 301 maritime and shipbuilding port fee suspension ends | Fees reinstate | Recalculate port cost exposure | 
| November 10, 2026 | 178 Section 301 exclusions expire | Duties reinstate on affected lines | Screen products against the exclusion list | 
| November 10, 2026 | China’s rare earth export controls begin | New export license requirements take effect | Assess rare earth supply chain exposure | 
| January 10, 2027 | Broader U.S.-China truce expires (if not extended) | Potential tariff reinstatement | Model contingency scenarios now | 
None of the November dates are contingent on how the truce plays out. These are standstills ending on their own terms, on a date two months earlier than the headline suggests.
Of the four November measures in the table above, the 178 Section 301 exclusions are the one most directly tied to the tariff-relief conversation. They cover specific products that have been carved out of Section 301 duties since 2018 and 2019. Unless USTR extends them again, entries filed on or after November 10 lose that carve-out and revert to standard Section 301 rates. The BIS Affiliates Rule and the port fee suspension are separate tracks entirely, with their own November 9 expiration, unrelated to the tariff-relief framework or the truce.
Add to that a separate, earlier deadline: China’s more expansive rare earth export controls, the ones claiming authority over goods made anywhere in the world using Chinese-origin rare earths exceeding 0.1% of the item’s value at the component level, take effect for the first time on November 10 as well. That’s not part of the 30-for-30 deal at all, and the September summit didn’t extend it.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal stated that India is poised to become a global car manufacturing hub as growing demand makes local production viable. He noted that trade deals protect the mass-market vehicle segment while luxury carmakers expand operations.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has expressed confidence that India could emerge as a global car manufacturing hub as demand grows enough to make local production commercially viable for international automakers.
Speaking at the ‘Dilli Dialogue: Policies for a Future-Ready India’ in New Delhi, Goyal said the import quotas permitted under India’s trade agreements with the United Kingdom and the European Union largely cover expensive cars, while the mass-market segment for vehicles priced below ₹17 lakh remains protected.
He cited luxury carmakers setting up manufacturing plants in Pune after initially testing the Indian market as an example of how international manufacturers could expand production in India as demand grows.
Goyal also said European Union regulations could make car manufacturing in the bloc less competitive and encourage companies to shift more production to India.
“Tatas had so much trouble after they bought Jaguar. Tata Motors itself was going to collapse and then they put in a lot of re-engineering, and shift some models to India. Finally they were able to make money after years,” he said.
Electronics, tourism and jobs
Goyal said India needed a two-pronged approach: adopting the world's best technologies while identifying sectors with significant potential to create jobs and businesses.
He pointed to rising demand for electronics and white goods as an opportunity to attract investment into domestic manufacturing, including semiconductor fabrication plants.
Tourism, he said, was another sector with considerable potential to generate employment and create new business opportunities. Artificial intelligence could make tourism promotion more efficient, but human experiences would remain central to the industry.
“AI can only add to the efficiency of promoting tourism. But otherwise, human experiences will always be AI proof,” he said.
India’s workforce and trade strategy
Highlighting India's demographic advantage, Goyal referred to demand for Indian workers in countries such as Germany and Japan. He said people from the North-East could serve as India's brand ambassadors in nursing and caregiving, while describing the region as a gateway to ASEAN and the Far East.
Goyal said he had participated in 10 bilateral meetings with foreign counterparts on the sidelines of the G20 meeting in the US last month. He added that he was scheduled to meet ministers from the UK and Canada in New Delhi on October 12 and 13, respectively.
He also criticised trade decisions taken by the previous United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government, referring to a Cabinet resolution on Vietnam's market-economy status and free trade agreements involving the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) and ASEAN.
Goyal said India had trade agreements with Australia, New Zealand, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) and the European Union that excluded dairy products to protect the interests of small farmers.
He added that he did not believe other trade ministers viewed politeness as a sign of weakness.

articles.title: Amata CEO Vikrom Kromadit built his industrial park empire in Thailand and Vietnam. Laos is next - Fortune
articles.summary: Amata CEO Vikrom Kromadit built his industrial park empire in Thailand and Vietnam. Laos is next  Fortune
articles.full_text:
Thai real estate developer Amata Corporation says Laos will become its “largest focus” in the years to come, CEO Vikrom Kromadit tells Fortune.
“Laos will become our largest focus because of the land bank that they have,” Kromadit tells Fortune. “They also have lots of green energy—that’s why they’re called the battery of Southeast Asia.”
Amata expanded into Laos in 2022, starting with Amata City Namor, which covers 31.5 square kilometers and sits beside a station on the China-Laos Railway. The company says its long-term Laos vision could reach 200 square kilometers.
Kromadit’s company built its fortunes in Thailand and Vietnam. Amata Corporation, founded in 1989, built industrial parks across Thailand’s Rayong and Chon Buri provinces. It was also an early backer of Vietnam, building its first facility there in 1994, early in the Southeast Asian country’s reform program. Laos, however, offers an opportunity for Amata to capture Chinese manufacturers expanding to new manufacturing hubs in Southeast Asia.
Laos, Southeast Asia’s only landlocked country, boasts a huge energy surplus, as its rivers and mountainous terrain supported a government-led push to build hydroelectric dams as a core economic pillar. The country currently exports about 80% of its electricity to other Asian countries like Thailand, China, and Singapore.
“They have plenty of land and a lot of water,” Kromadit says, adding that it has “the best natural conditions” for industrial development. (While Laos generates over 12 GW of capacity from over 80 hydro plants, most cross-border transmission lines bypass local communities, sticking consumers with frequent blackouts.)
To Kromadit, Laos’s potential is also backed by China, long the country’s top foreign investor. In 2025, China pumped $18 billion into Laos’s economy, primarily toward industry, mining, and agriculture, according to the Vientiane Times, a local newspaper.
Laos has been slotted into “China plus one” supply chains, where both Chinese and global manufacturers move some—or all—of their production to other countries, both to reduce cost and avoid tariffs on Chinese-origin products.
“China is the largest manufacturer of all products, so they can’t just keep building only within their country,” Kromadit explains. “They’re also being hit by political pressure from the U.S.”
After graduating from National Taiwan University with a degree in mechanical engineering, he returned to Thailand in 1975 and founded V&K Enterprise, an import-export business that focused on agricultural products, minerals, and seafood. But by the 1980s, he was frustrated with being “just a middleman.”
“I wanted to make more money,” Kromadit confesses. “When I was in the food business, even though I was the one who created all the channels and brought in business, once companies achieved success, they kicked me out.”
In 1988, he cofounded the Bang Pakong Industrial Estate on the eastern coast of Bangkok, then established Amata Corporation in 1989. Amata’s first industrial facility, Amata City Chon Buri, opened that same year.
After Kromadit visited Vietnam in 1990, he decided to make the country Amata’s first overseas market. “I found that the Vietnamese were focused, capable, and smart,” he says. “I thought that Vietnam, in the future, would compete with Thailand for industrial investments.” Amata launched Amata City Bien Hoa in Dong Nai province in 1994.
His prediction has largely come true: Vietnam is now Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing economy, with Q3 GDP growth of 9.95%. Hanoi wants to have Vietnam reach high-income status by 2045.
Amata today hosts more than 1,500 factories in 12 locations across Thailand, Vietnam, and Laos. It briefly attempted an expansion into Myanmar in 2019, with a facility in Yangon, the country’s commercial center. Plans were halted in early 2021 following a military coup and resulting civil war.
Amata positions its facilities as industrial cities that include not just factories but also housing, schools, hospitals, and shopping malls. The company’s flagship Chon Buri campus, for instance, houses the massive 38,000-square-meter Lotus Plus Mall, which includes a hypermarket, retail stores, banks, restaurants, and an international cinema.
The company’s facilities include kindergartens, schools, and technical training institutes, with more on the way. “We’re now looking to build a university,” Kromadit says.
Asked whether Amata might expand into other Southeast Asian markets, like Indonesia or Cambodia, Kromadit says the company already has enough land to occupy him for the rest of his life.
“The land that we have on hand is around 700 square kilometers,” he says. “It’s big enough to make me busy until I go to heaven.”

Investment Pipeline Accelerates
Investment approvals in the Philippines reached ₱297.14 billion by the end of September 2026, leaving the country just ₱13.86 billion short of surpassing the 2012 record of ₱311 billion, according to data from the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA). The agency tracks investment commitments across special economic zones that account for a substantial portion of the country's manufacturing base.
The surge in approvals comes as merchandise exports climbed 15 per cent year-on-year to US$64.04 billion during the January-August period, with electronics and semiconductors accounting for the bulk of shipments. August alone recorded US$9.11 billion in exports, the highest monthly figure for 2026 and a signal that production capacity is keeping pace with global demand for chips and electronic components.
Electronics manufacturing has long anchored the Philippines' export economy, but the current cycle reflects both demand-side strength and supply-side expansion. Multinational firms have accelerated investment in assembly and test facilities across Luzon and parts of Visayas, responding to persistent semiconductor shortages and efforts by end-customers to diversify supply chains beyond Northeast Asia.
Conversion Timeline in Focus
Approved investments do not immediately translate into operational capacity. The gap between PEZA approval and actual construction, equipment imports, hiring and production ramp-up typically spans 12 to 24 months, depending on project scale and sector. Industrial property developers, logistics operators and power utilities have reported stronger enquiries, but concrete capex commitments remain concentrated in a handful of large-scale projects rather than broad-based activity.
For the Philippines to reach the US$100 billion annual export target that policymakers have flagged, monthly shipments would need to average around US$9 billion through the final quarter of 2026. August's performance suggests that threshold is achievable if electronics demand holds, though any softening in global semiconductor orders or delays in converter projects would weigh on both export momentum and the realisation of approved investments.
The external balance has improved modestly as export growth outpaces import growth in key categories, though the Philippines remains a net importer of capital goods, fuel and raw materials. A sustained acceleration in exports would ease pressure on the current account and provide more room for monetary policy adjustments if inflation dynamics allow.
Regional Competition Intensifies
The Philippines competes directly with Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia for electronics investment, and approval figures alone do not guarantee market share gains. Vietnam's electronics exports exceeded US$100 billion in 2025, supported by established supply chains, infrastructure investment and a larger pool of industrial land. Thailand has leveraged automotive electronics and hard-disk drive legacy to attract next-generation semiconductor packaging projects, while Malaysia continues to dominate in backend assembly and test.
PEZA's approval pipeline includes projects in semiconductors, data centre components and electric vehicle subassemblies, but execution risk remains elevated. Power reliability, logistics bottlenecks at Manila's ports and skilled labour availability are recurring constraints cited by investors. Industrial property developers have responded by expanding off-port logistics hubs and securing dedicated power allocations, yet infrastructure gaps persist in secondary zones outside Metro Manila and Cavite.
Banking sector exposure to manufacturing capex has increased, with several large lenders reporting growth in project finance and working capital facilities for electronics and industrial clients. Credit quality in the segment has remained stable, though concentration risk would rise if a significant portion of approved projects fail to reach financial close or encounter construction delays.
Outlook Hinges on Execution
The convergence of strong export data and near-record investment approvals presents a favourable backdrop for industrial sectors, but the Philippines has seen approval cycles before that did not fully convert into capacity additions. Policymakers have streamlined permitting for PEZA-registered projects, yet local government coordination, utility connections and customs clearance for imported equipment remain variables that can extend timelines.
If September and fourth-quarter export figures sustain the August pace, the US$100 billion milestone would mark a psychological and practical threshold, reinforcing the case for further manufacturing investment. Conversely, any downturn in global electronics demand or project cancellations would dampen both near-term export performance and medium-term capacity expansion, leaving the investment pipeline vulnerable to the same external shocks that have disrupted previous cycles.
Industrial property, logistics, power generation and banks with manufacturing exposure stand to benefit if conversion rates improve and export momentum persists. The next six months will clarify whether this cycle differs from past approval surges that faded before reaching full-scale production.

Quartz Market Overview
Quartz is a naturally occurring mineral composed primarily of silicon dioxide (SiO₂). It is among the most abundant minerals in the Earth's crust and is used across numerous industrial sectors because of its durability, hardness, chemical inertness, and resistance to high temperatures.
Commercial quartz production generally involves mining, crushing, screening, sizing, and washing to obtain materials with the required particle size and quality. Depending on the intended application, additional beneficiation and purification processes may be necessary. High-purity quartz undergoes more advanced processing to reduce impurities and achieve the quality specifications required for semiconductor manufacturing, solar photovoltaics, optical fiber, and specialty glass.
The quartz market includes natural and synthetic quartz products in various forms, such as crystals, powders, granules, sand, pebbles, and quartz glass. Natural quartz is widely used in construction, glass manufacturing, ceramics, foundry applications, and engineered-stone surfaces. Synthetic and processed quartz products serve applications requiring specific material characteristics and performance standards.
Demand for quartz varies according to purity, form, and end-use requirements. Conventional industrial applications benefit from the availability and affordability of natural quartz, whereas advanced manufacturing sectors require specialized materials with carefully controlled impurity levels.
The market is also influenced by developments across the semiconductor and renewable energy supply chains. Semiconductor fabrication requires quartz components capable of withstanding elevated temperatures and chemically aggressive environments. Similarly, crystalline silicon photovoltaic manufacturing uses high-purity quartz in crucibles and related processing equipment.
Key Growth Drivers of the Quartz Market
Expansion of Semiconductor Manufacturing
The expansion of semiconductor manufacturing is a major driver of the global quartz market, particularly for high-purity quartz and fused quartz products. Quartz is used in semiconductor processing equipment because of its thermal stability, chemical resistance, and ability to maintain low contamination levels under demanding operating conditions.
Quartz components, including crucibles, tubes, boats, rings, and other specialized equipment, are used during silicon processing and wafer manufacturing. These components may be exposed to high temperatures and corrosive chemicals, creating demand for materials with consistent quality and reliable performance.
As semiconductor manufacturers expand production to meet demand for processors, memory devices, power electronics, and other integrated circuits, demand for specialized quartz components is expected to increase. New fabrication facilities and the expansion of existing plants across Asia, North America, and Europe are creating opportunities for suppliers of high-quality quartz materials.
The increasing complexity of semiconductor manufacturing is further strengthening the importance of material purity. Even small concentrations of metallic or other impurities can affect silicon purity and manufacturing performance. Consequently, quartz suppliers are focusing on beneficiation, purification, and quality-control processes to meet stringent industrial requirements.
These conditions create opportunities for suppliers capable of securing suitable raw-material deposits and consistently delivering high-purity quartz products. Continued technological advancement in semiconductor manufacturing is expected to support demand for specialized quartz materials throughout the forecast period.
Rising Solar Photovoltaic Production
The expansion of solar photovoltaic manufacturing is another significant factor supporting quartz market growth. High-purity quartz is used in the production of quartz crucibles required for melting and growing crystalline silicon ingots. In the Czochralski process, these crucibles support silicon crystal growth, after which the ingots are cut into wafers and processed into solar cells.
Growing adoption of renewable energy is encouraging investment in photovoltaic manufacturing capacity. Governments and industrial companies are expanding solar power deployment to support decarbonization objectives and improve energy security.
