articles.title: AI Boom Opens New Growth Opportunities for Philippine Semiconductor Industry, FedEx Report Finds - FedEx newsroom
articles.summary: AI Boom Opens New Growth Opportunities for Philippine Semiconductor Industry, FedEx Report Finds  FedEx newsroom
articles.full_text:
Manila, Philippines, October 12, 2026 – Federal Express Corporation (FedEx), one of the world’s largest express transportation companies, released findings from a new report developed in collaboration with Frost & Sullivan examining the evolving semiconductor ecosystem across Asia Pacific (APAC).
The report finds that growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI), high-performance computing, electric vehicles (EVs), and advanced communications technologies is accelerating semiconductor production and driving investment in the digital infrastructure that powers the AI economy. These trends are creating increasingly complex regional and global supply chains that depend on speed, visibility, and resilience.
For the Philippines, the shift presents an opportunity to build on the country’s established position in the global semiconductor supply chain as an important hub for assembly, packaging and testing, supported by a skilled workforce and an established ecosystem of global manufacturers and local suppliers.
The report, From AI to EVs: How APAC Semiconductors Drive the Global Innovation Map, highlights how APAC has become the center of the global semiconductor ecosystem, accounting for approximately 58% of global semiconductor industry revenue. As industries increasingly rely on advanced chips to power AI applications, data centers, connected devices, and next-generation vehicles, the ability to move semiconductors and related technologies efficiently across multiple markets has become critical.
A recent FedEx survey conducted at SEMICON Taiwan 2026, one of the industry’s most influential trade shows, reinforced expectations for continued regional growth. Nearly four in five respondents identified Taiwan, Southeast Asia, Greater China, and Japan as the markets expected to see the greatest increase in semiconductor demand over the next three years.
“The next decade of innovation will be shaped not only by advances in semiconductors, but by the strength and resilience of the supply chains that power AI and digital infrastructure,” said Salil Chari, president, Asia Pacific, FedEx. “As investment in AI infrastructure accelerates, businesses are managing increasingly complex supply chains spanning semiconductors, servers, networking equipment, cooling systems and advanced technology components across multiple markets. Resilience, visibility, and agility have become strategic advantages. FedEx is helping customers connect these critical supply chains through our extensive APAC network, global reach and specialized logistics capabilities, enabling innovation to move faster from factory floor to data center.”
AI Infrastructure a Major Driver of Semiconductor Demand
The report identifies AI and high-performance computing as the fastest-growing drivers of semiconductor demand. More than 2,000 new data centers are expected to be built globally between 2026 and 2035.
Beyond semiconductors, AI is accelerating demand for an entire ecosystem of supporting infrastructure including high-density servers, networking equipment, cooling systems and power solutions. These critical technologies often move multiple manufacturing, assembly and testing hubs before being deployed in AI data centers worldwide, creating increasingly interconnected supply chains.
As a result, businesses are placing greater emphasis on logistics providers that can deliver speed, visibility and seamless cross-border connectivity for high-value, time-sensitive shipments.
At the same time, EVs, which require significantly more chips than traditional vehicles, together with 5G, IoT, consumer electronics, medical devices and industrial automation are further expanding semiconductor demand across industries.
The Philippines: A Key Player In Increasingly Interconnected APAC Semiconductor Ecosystem
The report highlights APAC’s central role in semiconductor innovation and production. Rather than being concentrated in a single market, semiconductor manufacturing is distributed across highly specialized hubs throughout the region. Key regional strengths include:
China as a major material supplier, consumer market and growing fabrication hub; Taiwan, which leads global advanced semiconductor manufacturing and accounts for roughly 60% of worldwide foundry output; South Korea, a global leader in memory chip production and advanced fabrication capabilities; and Japan plays a critical role in semiconductor equipment, materials and specialty manufacturing inputs.
Southeast Asia, including the Philippines, has emerged as a key center for semiconductor assembly, packaging and testing operations.
The Philippines hosts manufacturing operations of major global semiconductor companies and has developed a skilled workforce supporting assembly, packaging and testing services. This existing industry base gives the country an opportunity to capture new investment as semiconductor companies seek to expand and diversify their manufacturing and sourcing footprints across Asia Pacific.
Recent investment activity in the country is highlighting this shift. Philippine economic zones continue to attract electronics and advanced manufacturing projects, while government efforts are increasingly focused on moving the country toward higher-value activities within the semiconductor value chain, including research, engineering, design, and advanced manufacturing.
This specialization creates a deeply interconnected ecosystem, with semiconductor design, fabrication, packaging, testing and deployment often occurring across multiple countries before a final product reaches market. Alongside hyperscalers, Small and Medium Sized Enterprises (SMEs) also play an important role, benefiting from growing opportunities in high-value niche segments.
“The Philippines has decades of experience and a strong talent base in semiconductor manufacturing. The opportunity now is to build on these strengths as the industry enters a new phase driven by AI, advanced computing and increasingly distributed supply chains,” said Garrick Thompson, managing director, FedEx Philippines. “For the Philippines to capture more of this growth, manufacturing capability needs to be matched by reliable connectivity to suppliers and customers across the region and around the world. This is where logistics can help turn our geographic position and industrial capabilities into a stronger competitive advantage.”
Industry sentiment reflects this regionalization trend. In the FedEx SEMICON Taiwan survey, 35% of respondents said they expect their companies to expand manufacturing into additional APAC markets over the next three years. A further 25% plan to increase or diversify sourcing either within APAC or globally.
Supply Chains Shift from Efficiency to Resilience
Supply chain resilience is becoming a strategic priority. Geopolitical uncertainty, regulatory complexity, and other external disruptions continue to challenge operations.
Survey findings reinforce this shift with 30% of respondents citing geopolitical disruption as the most significant challenge to growth ahead of rising operating costs and cross-border trade and customs complexity.
Consequently, traditional just-in-time operating models are being supplemented with more resilient supply chain strategies, including geographic diversification and inventory buffers. This evolution is increasing demand for reliable international logistics networks capable of supporting high-value, critical shipments.
Logistics Enabling the Next Chapter of Semiconductor Growth
As semiconductor supply chains become more complex and globally interconnected, survey findings suggest that speed and visibility will be central to future logistics strategies, with 44% of respondents identifying faster international shipping as the most important capability when selecting logistics and supply chain partners over the next three years.
FedEx supports this connectivity through its extensive international network and operations in the Philippines, including its gateway at Clark. Located close to major industrial and economic zones in Central Luzon, Clark provides Philippine businesses with convenient access to FedEx’s regional and global network, helping facilitate the movement of high-value and time-sensitive shipments to international markets.
The report provides businesses with insights into the evolving AI and semiconductor ecosystem across Asia Pacific, helping them better understand emerging supply chain trends, growth opportunities and the logistics capabilities needed to support the next wave of innovation. India's automobile industry is gearing up for a potential record year as festive demand rises across petrol-powered and electric vehicles, even as geopolitical uncertainties and global supply chain challenges continue, Vikram Kasbekar, Executive Director of Hero MotoCorp told ANI.
Speaking with reporters on the sidelines of CII's 17th Visionary Leaders for Manufacturing conference in Mumbai, Kasbekar said demand has outpaced supply in both internal combustion engine and electric vehicle segments, creating an opportunity for manufacturers to increase production.
"This is an opportunity that has come after a long time, when the industry has not been able to supply enough to meet demand. The situation is improving, and the automobile industry is gearing up to meet market requirements. Hopefully, this will be a record year for the industry," he said.
On the impact of global conflicts and rising commodity prices, Kasbekar said the company was prepared to manage cost pressures and meet market demand. He noted that fluctuations in commodity prices remain a concern but said Hero MotoCorp had not faced any significant challenges so far. The company is also expanding its electric vehicle business under the VIDA brand he stated. "There are definitely pressures from a commodity standpoint, and this is something we need to be prepared for. Such uncertainties are always a possibility. However, so far, we have not faced any significant problems and are well-equipped to meet market requirements," Kasbekar said.
On supply chain challenges, particularly the availability of semiconductors and microcontrollers used in vehicles, he said companies were following their own sourcing strategies based on the specific components required for their products. Kasbekar added that manufacturers identify the processors, controllers and other components needed for their vehicles before deciding how to source them. Insider Spotlight
The report, The World Rewired: Shifts in Global Trade and Foreign Direct Investment, published by Citi Institute and Citi Services, found that 72 percent of corporations consider releasing trapped liquidity their top priority over the next 12 months, up from 66 percent earlier in 2026.
Why it matters
Companies are shifting their focus from supply chain diversification toward unlocking cash tied up in operations to strengthen financial resilience.
"For several years the conversation was dominated by resilience through diversification," Citi Services global head of trade and working capital solutions Adoniro Cestari said in a statement.
"Companies diversified their supplier base and redesigned sourcing strategies to strengthen their operations. Now treasury teams are turning to a related question: where is our cash sitting, and how quickly can it be put to work?"
By the numbers
Citi's payment data showed global flows increasing 40 percent year-on-year during the first half of 2026, with technology-related payments climbing 50 percent.
Asia and Latin America recorded technology payment growth of 60 percent and 58 percent, respectively, reflecting expanding investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Meanwhile, 68 percent of corporations identified rising input costs as a major working capital concern, while 59 percent cited elevated interest rates.
Digital transformation accelerates
Artificial intelligence adoption in trade operations surged from 16 percent in 2024 to 45 percent in 2026.
Nearly half of surveyed corporations are also evaluating blockchain and distributed ledger technologies to improve financial visibility and efficiency.
The bigger picture
Trade routes are evolving rather than disappearing, with companies increasingly diversifying markets while strengthening cash management.
The findings draw on Citi's global payments network and surveys involving more than 700 large corporations and 150 suppliers.
The report underscores how treasury management, digital innovation and liquidity optimization are becoming central to corporate competitiveness amid persistent global uncertainty. —Ramon C. Nocon | Ed: Corrie S. Narisma

With positive results in attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), along with the orientation towards developing industrial infrastructure, improving the quality of human resources, and promoting administrative reform, Thai Nguyen province is gradually building an important foundation to realize the goal of double-digit economic growth.
FDI continues to affirm its role as a driver of growth.
In the first nine months of 2026, Thai Nguyen recorded positive results in attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), with a total newly registered and increased capital of US$8,052.9 million. This included 23 newly licensed FDI projects with a total registered capital of US$5,811.05 million; and 22 projects with adjusted capital increases, adding US$2,241.85 million. As of September 30, 2026, the province had a cumulative total of 251 FDI projects with a total registered capital of US$19.406 billion.
The above figures demonstrate Thai Nguyen's attractiveness to international investors and reflect the trend of expanding production and business activities of enterprises already present in the locality. Capital continues to flow into the fields of electronics, component and circuit board manufacturing, processing and manufacturing industries, and high technology, creating momentum to promote the shift in economic structure towards industrialization and modernization.
For achieving double-digit growth targets, FDI is crucial in many aspects. Firstly, attracting large-scale projects contributes to supplementing investment resources, expanding industrial production capacity, and increasing export value. Once these projects become operational, the demand for labor, logistics services, transportation, trade, and supporting industries also increases, creating a ripple effect on the local economy.
Furthermore, the continued increase in capital by existing investors demonstrates the potential for expanding production and maintaining the competitiveness of the investment environment. This provides a basis for Thai Nguyen to consolidate its growth momentum in the medium and long term, instead of relying solely on attracting new projects.
However, for FDI to truly become a driving force for rapid and sustainable growth, it requires not only an increase in the scale of registered capital, but also improvements in the quality of disbursement, production efficiency, budget contributions, job quality, and connectivity between FDI enterprises and domestic businesses.
One of the highlights in Thai Nguyen's investment attraction strategy is the development of electronics, semiconductor, and high-tech projects in the Yen Binh Industrial Park. Spanning 197.61 hectares and with a total investment exceeding 3,500 billion VND, the project is envisioned as a "Pioneering Urban Technology Complex," integrating hardware and software production with centers for finance, commerce and services, research and development (R&D), education and training, and housing for experts.

This model opens up a new approach to industrial development, where production infrastructure is connected to an ecosystem of research, training, and support services. Through this, businesses can improve operational efficiency, access suitable human resources, and enhance their innovation capabilities.
This is also a significant step towards the province's goal of double-digit growth. Developing high-tech industries not only creates additional production capacity but also opens up opportunities to increase added value, improve labor productivity, and promote technology transfer. If implemented comprehensively, Thai Nguyen can gradually transform from a center for electronics manufacturing to a hub for the development of electronics, semiconductor industries, and research and development activities.
In reality, operations in industrial zones show that many businesses maintain high production capacity thanks to stable orders, while proactively diversifying their supply sources and enhancing their competitiveness in the face of fluctuations in the international market.
Ms. Tu Chi Yen, Deputy Director of Human Resources at RQ Technology Vietnam, stated: Thai Nguyen has the advantage of its geographical location and transportation system, especially the expressways, which help businesses connect conveniently with Hanoi , economic centers, and seaports. This contributes to saving time and logistics costs, improving operational efficiency, and strengthening business confidence. Therefore, businesses have decided to invest and develop long-term in the locality.
Creating room for sustainable growth.
Recognizing that the competition to attract FDI is increasingly shifting from incentives to the ability to meet investors' requirements, Mr. Nguyen The Hoan, Head of the Management Board of Industrial Parks in Thai Nguyen province, said: The locality is stepping up investment promotion in a professional and focused manner, strengthening coordination with central ministries and agencies, and expanding cooperation with international investment promotion organizations and business associations such as KORCHAM, KOTRA, JETRO, AmCham Vietnam, EuroCham, and the Taiwan Business Association in Vietnam.
In addition, the province focuses on improving industrial park infrastructure, transportation, electricity, logistics, and digital infrastructure. According to the plan, Thai Nguyen has 37 industrial parks with a total area of nearly 14,000 hectares, along with a concentrated information technology park of about 200 hectares. This is an important foundation for preparing land, technical infrastructure, and conditions to receive large-scale high-tech projects.

High-quality human resources are also identified as a key factor. Strengthening the links between the State, schools, and businesses, prioritizing the training of human resources in the fields of semiconductors, electronics, artificial intelligence, data science , automation, and digital technology will contribute to meeting production needs while enhancing the participation of local labor in high value-added processes.
Simultaneously, administrative reform, digital transformation , expansion of online public services, and the implementation of a "green channel" mechanism for key projects continue to be necessary solutions to shorten processing times, reduce compliance costs, and enhance the transparency of the investment environment.
In the journey to realize double-digit economic growth, attracting high-quality FDI is one of the important drivers, but the ultimate effectiveness depends on the ability to transform capital flows into production capacity, technology, labor productivity, and real added value. With a focus on developing high-tech industries, investing in synchronized infrastructure, improving human resource quality, and enhancing the business environment, Thai Nguyen is gradually consolidating its foundation for faster, more sustainable growth and deeper participation in the global value chain.

“For AVL, the opportunity is broader than a potential new source of vanadium demand,” he said. “We see strategic alignment between Australian critical minerals, Tyfast’s US-developed battery technology and the increasing focus on secure and resilient supply chains across Australia, the United States and other markets seeking supply chain diversification.”
Tyfast is developing LVO-based lithium-ion batteries designed to combine rapid charging, long cycle life, broad temperature performance and high energy density for demanding heavy-duty applications.
The company has reported charging to more than 80% state of charge in under six minutes at room temperature and under 11 minutes at -20°C in 3 Ah pouch cells, with energy density of about 200-250 Wh/kg.
Its wider development program has also demonstrated more than 10,000 cycles in smaller-format test cells and operation across temperatures ranging from -40°C to +70°C.
These performance metrics could be particularly well suited for defence, heavy-duty transportation, construction and other industrial applications where charging downtime, operating conditions and intensive duty cycles can limit conventional lithium-ion battery performance.
Under the MOU, AVL and Tyfast will undertake technical and commercial evaluation of Australian vanadium oxide, including determining target product specifications and assessing potential quantities and delivery schedules.
The program is expected to include sample testing, bench and pilot-scale qualification, potential mine-site and fleet trials and engagement with original equipment manufacturers.
Successful technical and commercial evaluation could lead to demonstration projects, pre-commercial supply and negotiations for longer-term commercial supply or offtake agreements.

articles.title: Minister urges ‘drastic’ action to cut reliance on imports amid review of China trade deficit - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Minister urges ‘drastic’ action to cut reliance on imports amid review of China trade deficit  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): The government must take “drastic” action to reduce its reliance on imports and strengthen domestic manufacturing, said Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani.
He said specifically, the government is reviewing products that contribute to Malaysia's large trade deficit with China, including goods that were once made locally.
Johari did not specify the measures being considered or their implementation timeline.
“We have held many engagement sessions with local companies. Although they disagree, we must take very drastic action for the country’s long-term benefit, to protect our economy without depending on countries that we believe could adversely affect our economy as a whole,” Johari said during oral question time in the Dewan Rakyat on Monday.
The trade minister was responding to Datuk Adnan Abu Hassan (BN-Kuala Pilah), who asked about Malaysia’s exposure to trade tensions and new tariffs arising from its concentration on major trade markets, such as the US and China.
Adnan also asked how the government would ensure export diversification developed higher-value added products, instead of merely expanding assembly or processing activities with limited domestic value added.
According to data from the Department of Statistics and the Ministry of Economy, Malaysia had a trade surplus of RM101.5 billion with the US in 2025, and a trade deficit of RM163.4 billion with China in the same period.
In the first eight months of 2026, Malaysia's trade deficit with China stood at RM159.8 billion, the data showed.
In plain terms, Malaysia sells far more to the US than it buys from it, but buys far more from China than it sells to it.
The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry will examine why some products previously made by Malaysian companies were now being imported, and whether domestic manufacturers could resume producing them, he said.
He argued that relying on cheaper imports could undermine local manufacturing capacity. Once domestic factories closed, products previously imported at low prices could become more expensive, he added.
“We can no longer simply allow imports as the easy way out,” Johari said. The government would identify sectors requiring support to produce raw materials and semi-finished goods locally, with small and medium enterprises playing a greater role in supplying exporters.
Responding separately to a supplementary question from Permatang Pauh MP Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad on domestic value added in electrical and electronics (E&E) exports, Johari cited RM712 billion in E&E exports and RM567 billion in imports last year, resulting in a sectoral trade surplus of about RM145 billion.
For non-E&E products, he cited exports of RM897 billion and imports of RM885 billion, leaving a much smaller surplus of RM12 billion.
Johari said Malaysia’s semiconductor companies should expand beyond conventional assembly, testing and packaging into advanced packaging. He acknowledged that Malaysia’s substantial exposure to E&E exports left it vulnerable to a downturn in the global semiconductor cycle, changes in technology, supply-chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions.
A sharp downturn could trigger inventory adjustments and production cuts, weighing on national exports, particularly if growth in other sectors was insufficient to offset the decline, he said.
“The government’s approach is not to reduce the role of E&E and semiconductors, which are among Malaysia’s competitive strengths. Instead, we are managing the risks of this dependence through three main strategies,” he said.
These comprise strengthening the E&E value chain through activities such as integrated circuit design and advanced packaging; developing other high-value industries and domestic supply chains; and broadening export markets.

articles.summary: BOT sees exports and AI supporting 2.3% Thai growth in 2026  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
The Bank of Thailand (BOT) expects Thailand’s economy to grow by around 2.3% in 2026, supported by strong exports and investment linked to artificial intelligence (AI). Governor Vitai Ratanakorn warned, however, that longstanding structural weaknesses had reduced the country’s potential growth rate to about 2.7%.
Vitai’s assessment followed the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raising its 2026 growth forecast for Thailand to 2.1% from 1.9%. He said the BOT’s outlook was consistent with most analysts’ projections of between 2% and 2.3%.
Thai exports are expected to expand by 17–18%, making them a major driver of the BOT’s growth outlook for 2026, according to Vitai.
Vitai also identified private investment and foreign direct investment (FDI) as key drivers, citing expected growth of up to 13%, a high rate compared with previous years. He said the wave of AI-related activity was helping to sustain investment momentum.
Inflation is expected to be around 2.2%, according to Vitai, who described Thailand’s economy as relatively stable and highly resilient. He said growth momentum had continued despite various challenges, including the recent flooding.
Thailand’s potential growth rate has fallen to about 2.7%, according to Vitai. The measure describes the pace achievable when the country fully uses its available resources and technology.
Vitai warned that structural problems had progressively weakened Thailand’s economic performance, with actual growth slowing from 3–5% in the past to just over 2% today.
Decades of low investment, declining productivity and competitiveness in traditional industries, a shrinking workforce as the population ages, and weaknesses in the education system were among the constraints identified by Vitai.
High household debt and the burden of public debt also weighed on Thailand’s economy, Vitai said. He cited a household debt ratio of 86–87%, describing the level as among the highest in the world.
The BOT has expanded its role beyond monetary policy to help address Thailand’s structural weaknesses, support the economy, improve living standards and strengthen small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), according to Vitai.
Thailand’s structural problems cannot be resolved through a single project, Vitai said, calling for all relevant agencies to accelerate coordinated efforts to address them.

Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Bps Pressure Sensors market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global Bps Pressure Sensors market is entering a decade of structural expansion, with demand projected to accelerate through 2035. These electronic components, which convert pressure into analog or digital signals, are increasingly embedded in non-negotiable system architectures across industrial, automotive, medical, and consumer applications. The market is bifurcating into high-volume, cost-driven segments and high-reliability, performance-driven niches, each with distinct supply chains and qualification pathways.
Regulatory mandates, such as TPMS in automotive and stringent medical device approvals, are creating stable long-term demand pools, while industrial digitalization and IIoT adoption are pushing sensors from discrete components to intelligent, networked nodes. Value is migrating from bare sensor dies to integrated, application-ready modules, with competitive advantage shifting toward players with ASIC-based signal conditioning, advanced packaging, and software capabilities. Supply chain resilience remains a critical constraint, particularly for specialized MEMS fab capacity and automotive/medical-grade ASICs.
This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market, covering historical data from 2012 to 2025 and forward-looking scenarios to 2035, segmented by end-use sector, region, and product architecture.
The baseline scenario for the Bps Pressure Sensors market anticipates steady growth from 2026 to 2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.8%, bringing the market index to 176 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook assumes continued recovery in global industrial production, sustained automotive electrification and safety mandates, and accelerating adoption of IIoT and smart infrastructure. Demand will be strongest in Asia-Pacific, driven by manufacturing expansion and automotive production, while North America and Europe will see robust demand from medical devices, aerospace, and industrial automation.
The market will increasingly favor integrated, digital sensors with embedded diagnostics and wireless connectivity, as end-users seek predictive maintenance and data-rich ecosystems. Pricing pressure will persist in high-volume consumer and automotive segments, but high-reliability applications in medical and industrial safety will sustain premium margins. Supply chain constraints, particularly for MEMS fabrication and ASICs, may moderate growth in the short term, but capacity expansions and dual-sourcing strategies are expected to alleviate bottlenecks by the late 2020s.
Overall, the market is poised for resilient expansion, underpinned by regulatory mandates and systemic digitalization rather than pure economic cycles.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Regulatory mandates for tire pressure monitoring systems (TPMS) in automotive markets worldwide
- Rising adoption of industrial IoT and Industry 4.0 for predictive maintenance and process optimization
- Increasing demand for medical devices requiring precise pressure monitoring, such as ventilators and infusion pumps
- Growth in consumer electronics and wearables incorporating pressure sensors for altitude and environmental sensing
- Expansion of smart infrastructure and building automation systems for HVAC and water management
- Shift toward integrated, digital pressure sensors with embedded diagnostics and wireless connectivity
Potential Growth Constraints
- Supply chain bottlenecks in specialized MEMS fabrication and automotive/medical-grade ASIC procurement
- Lengthy qualification and certification processes, particularly for medical and automotive applications
- Price erosion in high-volume consumer and automotive segments due to intense competition
- Technical challenges in miniaturization and harsh-environment operation limiting adoption in extreme applications
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Automotive (estimated share: 32%)
The automotive sector remains the largest end-use market for Bps Pressure Sensors, underpinned by regulatory mandates for tire pressure monitoring systems (TPMS) in major markets and the increasing complexity of vehicle powertrains. Pressure sensors are critical for engine management, transmission control, brake systems, and HVAC, and are now integral to battery thermal management and hydrogen fuel cell systems in electric vehicles. Through 2035, demand will be propelled by the shift to electric and autonomous vehicles, which require more sensors for safety and efficiency. Design-in cycles are long, with qualification taking 2-3 years, creating stickiness for established suppliers.
Demand-side indicators include global light vehicle production, EV penetration rates, and regulatory updates on safety and emissions. The trend toward integrated sensor modules with digital outputs will accelerate, enabling vehicle-wide data networks. However, price pressure remains intense, and suppliers must balance cost with reliability to win platform awards. Current trend: Growing demand driven by TPMS mandates, vehicle electrification, and advanced driver assistance systems.
Major trends: TPMS mandates expanding to emerging markets, Electrification driving new pressure sensing applications in battery packs and thermal management, Integration of pressure sensors with temperature and humidity sensing in multi-parameter modules, Shift toward wireless sensors for reduced wiring harness complexity, and Increasing use of pressure sensors in autonomous vehicle braking and suspension systems.
Representative participants: Bosch Sensortec, Infineon Technologies, Sensata Technologies, Denso Corporation, Continental AG, and NXP Semiconductors.
Industrial (estimated share: 28%)
The industrial sector is a major and growing market for Bps Pressure Sensors, driven by the digitalization of manufacturing and process industries. These sensors are used in hydraulic and pneumatic systems, HVAC, water and wastewater management, and industrial safety systems. The push toward Industry 4.0 and IIoT is transforming demand from simple analog sensors to intelligent, networked devices that provide real-time data for predictive maintenance and process optimization. Through 2035, growth will be supported by investments in smart factories, energy efficiency, and environmental monitoring. Demand-side indicators include industrial capex, automation spending, and the adoption of wireless sensor networks.
The industrial segment values reliability, accuracy, and long-term stability, often requiring robust packaging and certification for hazardous environments. Suppliers with strong application engineering and support capabilities will thrive, while commodity sensor makers face margin pressure. Current trend: Accelerating adoption of IIoT and Industry 4.0 for process automation and predictive maintenance.
Major trends: Rising deployment of wireless pressure sensors in remote and hazardous locations, Integration of pressure sensing with flow and temperature for multi-variable measurement, Growing demand for sensors with digital interfaces (IO-Link, HART) for seamless integration, Increased focus on energy efficiency driving demand for pressure monitoring in HVAC and compressed air systems, and Expansion of sensor use in water management and environmental monitoring.
Representative participants: Honeywell International, TE Connectivity, Amphenol Corporation, Sensata Technologies, STMicroelectronics, and Kavlico (Amphenol).
Medical (estimated share: 18%)
The medical sector represents a high-value, high-reliability market for Bps Pressure Sensors, used in devices such as ventilators, infusion pumps, dialysis machines, and patient monitoring systems. Demand is driven by an aging global population, the rise of chronic diseases, and the shift toward home healthcare. Through 2035, growth will be supported by increasing healthcare expenditure, technological advancements in minimally invasive surgery, and the need for precise pressure monitoring in respiratory therapies. Regulatory approvals (FDA, CE) are stringent, creating high barriers to entry and long design-in cycles. Demand-side indicators include hospital admissions, procedure volumes, and home healthcare adoption rates.
Sensors must meet strict accuracy, biocompatibility, and sterilization requirements. The trend toward disposable and single-use sensors in some applications will create new opportunities, while integration with digital health platforms will enable remote patient monitoring. Current trend: Steady growth due to aging population, chronic disease management, and home healthcare.
Major trends: Growing demand for disposable pressure sensors in surgical and infusion applications, Integration of pressure sensors with wireless connectivity for remote patient monitoring, Miniaturization enabling catheter-based pressure sensing, Increasing use of pressure sensors in wearable health devices, and Rising adoption of home healthcare devices requiring reliable, low-power sensors.
Representative participants: Honeywell International, TE Connectivity, Merit Medical Systems, Sensata Technologies, Amphenol Corporation, and STMicroelectronics.
Consumer Electronics (estimated share: 12%)
Consumer electronics is a dynamic but price-sensitive end-use sector for Bps Pressure Sensors. These sensors are used in smartphones for altitude and weather sensing, in wearables for activity tracking and altitude measurement, and in smart home devices for HVAC and water leak detection. Through 2035, demand will be driven by the proliferation of IoT devices, the integration of pressure sensing in augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) headsets, and the growing popularity of outdoor and fitness wearables. articles.title: Updating our assumed commodity prices and fair values of the two largest Aussie miners - Morningstar Australia
articles.summary: Updating our assumed commodity prices and fair values of the two largest Aussie miners  Morningstar Australia
articles.full_text:
Stronger copper, aluminum and zinc prices offset by iron ore.
Copper trades near historical highs at about USD 6.50 per pound, up 10% since our July 2026 update, given mine supply disruptions and tariff-related trade distortions. Zinc and aluminum prices are also stronger, though near-term iron ore futures are little changed.
We update our iron ore and base metals mining coverage fair values based on our latest commodity price assumptions.
Stronger copper and aluminum prices see Rio Tinto’s fair value estimate increased
Along with stronger aluminum and alumina prices, no-moat Rio Tinto’s (ASX: RIO) fair value is up 4%, to $130.
Rio Tinto is one of the world’s largest miners with operations in iron ore, aluminum (including bauxite and alumina), copper, lithium, and minerals (mineral sands, borates, salt, diamonds). Commodity demand is tied to global economic growth, China’s in particular. Rio Tinto benefited greatly from the China boom over the past two decades. The firm’s largest customer by far is China, with about 60% of sales in 2025. We think the outlook is for earnings to decline, with demand for many commodities likely to soften with the end of the China boom, particularly iron ore, which has disproportionately benefited from the boom in infrastructure and real estate investment.
It has a large portfolio of long-lived assets with low operating costs, meaning it is one of the few miners profitable through the commodity cycle. Most revenue comes from operations in the relatively safe havens of Australia and North America. The invested capital base was inflated by substantial procyclical investment at the height of the China boom, including overpaying for Alcan. The subsequent iron ore expansion was also made when unit capital costs were high. These factors diluted returns to the point where we struggle to justify a moat. As a commodity producer, it is a price-taker, with the lack of pricing power reflected in cyclical commodity prices.
The recent focus has been to run a strong balance sheet, tightly control investments, and return cash to shareholders. Its purchase of lithium miner Arcadium in 2025 was modest for a firm of its size. It is also focused on winning back the trust of investors, regulators, and indigenous people on whose lands many of its mines are located after the destruction of the Juukan Gorge caves in 2020. Major expansion projects are the Oyu Tolgoi underground mine, Simandou, and expansion of the Pilbara iron ore system’s capacity from 330 million metric tons to between 345 and 360 million metric tons. Those projects are expected to be completed in the next few years. Otherwise, the focus is on incremental expansions through productivity and debottlenecking initiatives. These will be small but capital-efficient and should modestly improve unit costs and returns.
Stronger copper price sees BHP’s fair value increased, but more than reflected in share price
The higher copper price drives the 4% rise in no-moat BHP’s (ASX: BHP) estimate to $48.
BHP is the world’s largest miner by market capitalization. Its main operations span iron ore and copper, with smaller contributions from metallurgical coal and thermal coal. It placed its nickel operations on care and maintenance due to low prices in 2024. BHP is also developing its Jansen potash project in Canada. It merged its oil and gas assets with Woodside Energy in June 2022, vesting the Woodside shares it received to BHP shareholders and exiting the sector. It purchased copper miner Oz Minerals in fiscal 2023 and half of the Vicuña copper joint venture in fiscal 2025.
Commodity demand is tied to global economic growth, particularly China’s. BHP benefited greatly from the China boom over the past two decades. China is BHP’s largest customer, accounting for roughly 60% of sales in fiscal 2026. But we think demand for many commodities is likely to soften as the China boom ends, particularly for iron ore, which has disproportionately benefited from the boom in infrastructure and real estate investment.
Its generally low-cost, high-quality assets mean BHP is likely to be one of the few miners that remain profitable through the commodity cycle. Much of its operations are close to key Asian markets, particularly the low-cost iron ore business, providing a modest freight cost advantage relative to some producers such as those in Africa and South America.
BHP correctly values a strong balance sheet to provide some stability through the inevitable cycles and derives some modest benefit from commodity and geographic diversification. Much of its revenue comes from assets in the relatively safe haven of Australia. The development of Jansen in Canada is BHP’s major expansion project, while it is also looking to expand copper production. It is also pursuing modest expansion of its Western Australia Iron Ore operations above 305 million metric tons (100% basis) per year.
The good times during the height of the China boom saw significant capital expenditure, notably on iron ore and onshore US shale gas and oil. Overinvestment in the boom diluted returns to the point where we struggle to justify a moat. As a commodity producer, it lacks pricing power and is a price taker.

articles.title: ‘Malaysia must diversify beyond electrical and electronic exports’ - The Star
articles.summary: ‘Malaysia must diversify beyond electrical and electronic exports’  The Star
articles.full_text:
MALAYSIA must reduce its reliance on electrical and electronics (E&E) exports by diversifying into other high-value industries, says Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani.
The Investment, Trade and Industry Minister said this is crucial as the E&E sector accounted for 48.4% of the nation’s total exports from January to August, leaving it vulnerable to fluctuations in global semiconductor demand.
He noted that the semiconductor industry, in particular, is exposed to global economic conditions, technological changes, supply chain disruptions and geopolitical developments.
“These risks could lead to inventory depletion and lower output, putting pressure on E&E exports and the country’s overall export performance,” he said in reply to a question from Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad Jan (PN-Permatang Pauh).
Johari said Malaysia exported RM1.6 trillion worth of goods last year, of which RM712bil were E&E products.
Semiconductors, a major component of E&E exports, contributed RM483.6bil, or about 68% of the sector’s exports, during the first eight months of this year.
The government had implemented three key strategies to minimise the risks facing the E&E and semiconductor sectors.
The first was to strengthen and diversify the E&E value chain under the New Industrial Master Plan 2030 and the National Semiconductor Strategy.
The second strategy was to expand other high-value industries, including pharmaceuticals, automotive, aerospace, chemicals and petrochemicals, while strengthening domestic supply chains.
“Malaysia will also expand its export markets through the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (Matrade), targeting regions such as Central Asia, Africa and Latin America,” he said.
In response to a supplementary question from Datuk Adnan Abu Hassan (BN-Kuala Pilah), Johari said Malaysia needs to reduce its reliance on imported components and materials used to manufacture goods for export.
He said E&E exports totalled RM712bil in 2025, while the sector imported RM567bil, resulting in a trade surplus of RM145bil.
By comparison, non-E&E exports amounted to RM897bil, against imports of RM885bil, resulting in a surplus of RM12bil.
The government wants more local companies, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs), to produce components and semi-finished goods that are currently sourced abroad.

- Square Peg has closed more than A$1 bn across Fund 6 and Opportunities Fund 3, marking its largest fundraising round since its founding in 2012.
- Approximately 40% of the capital is allocated to early-stage investments, while 60% will support larger funding rounds involving existing portfolio companies and other growth-stage businesses.
- The fundraising strengthens Square Peg’s capacity to invest in AI, fintech and SaaS startups across Australia, Southeast Asia and Israel, while providing additional capital for promising portfolio companies.
Australian venture capital firm Square Peg has raised more than A$1 bn across two investment vehicles, completing its largest fundraising to date and expanding its capacity to back early-stage technology startups and established portfolio companies.
The capital was raised through Square Peg Fund 6, focused on early-stage investments, and Opportunities Fund 3, which provides larger investments to more mature businesses, including companies already within the firm’s portfolio.
Approximately 40% of the commitments were allocated to Fund 6, with the remaining 60% directed to Opportunities Fund 3. Square Peg confirmed that the combined amount exceeded A$1 bn but did not disclose the exact total or individual fund sizes.
The final closes were completed during the first half of 2026, according to the firm’s July investor letter. The latest fundraising exceeds the approximately A$860 mn secured in its separate 2022 fundraising round.
Founded in 2012 by Paul Bassat, a co-founder of employment marketplace SEEK, and former investment banker Tony Holt, Square Peg invests primarily in artificial intelligence, fintech and software-as-a-service companies.
Its investment strategy covers Australia and New Zealand, Southeast Asia and Israel, allowing the firm to support technology businesses across several markets and stages of development.
The two-fund structure addresses a common challenge for venture capital managers: balancing early-stage investment discipline with the capital requirements of successful companies as they expand.
Fund 6 enables Square Peg to make initial investments from seed through Series B without committing disproportionate amounts of capital to individual startups. Opportunities Fund 3 provides a separate pool for larger funding rounds, allowing the firm to maintain or increase its ownership in companies demonstrating strong commercial progress.
The arrangement also separates early-stage and growth-stage investment exposure for limited partners, whose risk preferences and investment objectives may differ.
The larger allocation to Opportunities Fund 3 indicates substantial capital availability for later-stage investments. It does not, however, mean that all of the new funding will be directed toward existing portfolio companies, as the vehicle can also invest in businesses outside the current portfolio.
For founders, the structure offers access to an investment firm capable of participating in successive financing rounds, potentially reducing the need to identify entirely new investors as capital requirements increase.
Existing Square Peg-backed companies may also benefit from additional funding capacity during a period when many startups remain affected by valuation adjustments, difficult fundraising conditions and extended timelines to liquidity.
Square Peg’s portfolio includes technology companies such as Canva, Airwallex, Rokt and Supabase, alongside investments in other fintech, enterprise software and AI businesses.
The firm’s investment and fundraising activities have involved Bassat and members of its broader team, including Leila Lee, who joined in 2017 as Head of Distribution and subsequently became a member of the Square Peg partnership.
The latest fundraising also provides evidence of institutional investor demand for established Australian venture capital managers operating internationally.
Square Peg’s allocation of approximately 60% to its opportunities vehicle places considerable emphasis on later-stage deployment, where companies may have more established business models but valuations and exit timing remain important risks.
The fundraising gives Square Peg additional capacity to support existing investments while continuing to identify new technology companies. The performance of the two vehicles will depend on investment selection, entry valuations, portfolio growth and the firm’s ability to generate exits across successive fund generations.

Salomon Puts Strategy Chief on the Executive Board
12/October/2026
As Salomon continues its rapid evolution from an Alpine heritage brand into a global sportswear titan, the French outdoor specialist is institutionalizing its growth plan. Salomon has promoted Katharina Bahde to Vice President of Global Strategy & Transformation and appointed her directly to the Salomon Executive Board.
The move elevates Bahde, who joined the company in September 2024 as Senior Director of Global Strategy & Transformation, into top-tier leadership alongside President Guillaume Meyzenq. By giving strategy a permanent, direct line to executive decision-making, Salomon is sending a clear message to the activewear sector: scaling up requires tight alignment between long-term vision and operational execution.
From Wall Street and Top-Tier Consulting to the French Alps
Bahde’s rapid ascent within Salomon highlights a broader talent migration across the outdoor industry, where technical outerwear and alpine heritage brands are increasingly recruiting from high-finance, elite consulting, and luxury retail to power global expansion.
Before joining Salomon, Bahde served as a Principal at Boston Consulting Group (BCG) and built her early career at Goldman Sachs, specializing in corporate transformation, strategy, and mergers and acquisitions.
"My work lies at the intersection of ambition and execution: defining the company's future strategic direction, globally and regionally, while ensuring the organisation is equipped to deliver on it." Katharina Bahde, VP of Global Strategy & Transformation
Salomon credited Bahde’s analytical rigor with helping the company navigate the complex, multi-channel demands of its recent expansion.
"In recent years, Katharina has played an increasingly important role in defining our strategic direction and strengthening our collaboration with Amer Sports. Her ability to turn complexity into clear and compelling strategic messages has greatly contributed to deepening understanding and buy-in for our priorities across Salomon." — Salomon Official Press Statement
The Strategic Context: Growth, Parent Synergies, and Market Evolution
Bahde’s elevation comes at a critical juncture for both Salomon and its parent company, Amer Sports (NYSE: AS), which also owns Arc’teryx and Wilson.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for expanding trade, investment and industrial cooperation with Thailand during talks with Thai Industry Minister Varawut Silpa-archa in Bangkok on Monday, October 12, 2026.
The meeting focused on strengthening economic relations between the two countries, encouraging joint manufacturing projects and attracting Thai investment to Egypt, particularly in the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE).
Abdelatty, who also serves as Minister of International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates, praised Thailand's industrial progress in innovation, digital transformation and sustainability.
He expressed Egypt's interest in drawing on Thai expertise to develop domestic manufacturing, increase local production and expand industrial exports.
Egypt and Thailand Discuss Joint Manufacturing Opportunities
During the meeting, Abdelatty called for greater exchanges of economic and trade delegations to explore investment opportunities and establish partnerships between Egyptian and Thai businesses.
He stressed the importance of improving access to both countries' markets and encouraging joint manufacturing in several priority industries, particularly rubber, petrochemicals and tyres, where Thailand has established industrial expertise.
The Egyptian minister also presented the investment opportunities available in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, citing its industrial facilities, ports, logistics infrastructure and strategic location near major international shipping routes.
He said Egypt's network of free trade agreements with several countries could provide Thai manufacturers with additional opportunities to reach markets in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.
Suez Canal Economic Zone Attracts Thai Investment
Abdelatty welcomed the investment by Thai company Hi-Tech Apparel, describing it as the first Thai industrial project in the Suez Canal Economic Zone.
The company is developing a $20 million sportswear manufacturing facility in the Qantara West industrial zone in Ismailia.
According to the SCZONE, the project covers approximately 64,000 square metres and is expected to create around 2,000 direct jobs.
Once fully operational, the facility is designed to produce approximately six million garments annually, primarily for export markets in Europe and the United States.
In March 2026, Hi-Tech Apparel reported progress on construction, with garment manufacturing facilities scheduled for completion in May and a fabric mill planned for later in the year.
Abdelatty said the investment could serve as a foundation for attracting additional Thai manufacturers to Egypt across other industrial sectors.
For his part, Silpa-archa welcomed the longstanding relations between Egypt and Thailand and expressed interest in expanding industrial, commercial and investment cooperation.
He described Egypt as a potential gateway to African, Arab and European markets and expressed Thailand's interest in exploring further manufacturing and investment opportunities within the Suez Canal Economic Zone.
The talks took place during Abdelatty's visit to Bangkok, the first by an Egyptian foreign minister in three decades, as both countries seek to develop closer economic and commercial relations.

articles.title: Nigeria’s lost purchasing power: How a decade of economic shocks changed money - Nairametrics

articles.full_text:
Nigeria’s economy has undergone a profound transformation over the past decade, with currency depreciation, rising inflation, fuel subsidy removal and high interest rates eroding household purchasing power even as nominal wages, government revenue and financial market valuations increased.
A report by Comercio Partners, titled The Decade That Changed Money, examines Nigeria’s economic performance between 2016 and 2026, highlighting how successive oil shocks, the COVID-19 pandemic, global conflicts and domestic policy changes reshaped the economy, investment decisions and the cost of living.
The report found that the naira lost nearly 90% of its dollar value between 2015 and 2024, while headline inflation peaked at 34.8% in December 2024.
Nigeria also spent more than N21 trillion on fuel subsidies between 2005 and 2023, according to the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative.

Although macroeconomic conditions have become more stable since the turbulence of 2023 and 2024, the report cautioned that stabilisation does not automatically translate into improved living standards.
Oil shocks, currency reforms and inflation
Nigeria’s economic challenges unfolded in three broad phases. Between 2016 and 2019, falling oil prices and disruptions to crude production triggered a recession, foreign exchange restrictions and rising inflation. The introduction of the Investors’ and Exporters’ foreign exchange window in 2017 supported a tentative recovery, but structural weaknesses persisted.
The COVID-19 pandemic caused another recession in 2020, prompting a ₦2.3 trillion Economic Sustainability Plan and monetary easing. While the economy returned to growth in 2021, the report argued that the recovery was shallow, with weak oil production and rising inflation undermining its benefits.
Between 2022 and 2026, global inflationary pressures, domestic supply constraints and long-delayed economic reforms converged. The removal of petrol subsidies in May 2023 and the unification of foreign exchange windows triggered sharp price and currency adjustments.
The Central Bank of Nigeria subsequently raised its Monetary Policy Rate from 11.5% in 2022 to 27.5% in 2024 to contain inflation and restore confidence. Inflation reached 34.8% in 2024, while the naira weakened to around ₦1,534 per dollar at the end of that year.
Conditions improved in 2025, when reported inflation fell to 15.15% by December following a rebasing of the Consumer Price Index. External reserves reached about $45 billion, while the naira strengthened. By May 2026, the report put the exchange rate at approximately ₦1,370 per dollar and the Nigerian Exchange All Share Index’s year-to-date gain at 55.7%.
However, the report noted that inflation began rising again in early 2026, demonstrating the economy’s continued vulnerability to external shocks.
Wages rise as household purchasing power falls
Despite successive minimum wage increases, the cost of essential goods and services has outpaced income growth for many Nigerians.
The national minimum wage rose from N18,000 in 2015 to N70,000 in 2024. However, the report estimated that cumulative inflation between 2020 and 2025 reached 152.7%, exceeding nominal minimum wage growth over the decade.
The pressure has been particularly severe in food, housing, transportation, education and healthcare. Food inflation reached 40.87% year-on-year in June 2024, while petrol prices climbed from approximately N87 per litre in 2015 to N1,239 in April 2025.
In Lagos, rents increased sharply, with some neighbourhoods recording increases of up to 200% over the 24 months leading to early 2026. The report estimated that rent could absorb about 70% of household income, significantly above the commonly cited 30% affordability benchmark.
The report also highlighted the growing burden of mobile data, school fees and medical expenses, with currency depreciation increasing the cost of imported inputs and services.
These pressures have forced households to cut spending, defer medical treatment, move to cheaper neighbourhoods and adjust consumption. The report noted that lower inflation does not mean prices have fallen, but rather that they are increasing more slowly.
Investors shift from yield to wealth preservation
Nigeria’s financial markets also experienced a fundamental shift as investors responded to currency weakness and persistent inflation.
Treasury bills and other fixed income instruments frequently delivered negative real returns between 2020 and 2025. In 2024, for example, the average one-year Treasury bill yield was 16%, against inflation of 33.2%, resulting in a negative real return of approximately 17.2%.
Equities performed better in several years, with the NGX All Share Index returning 51.2% in 2025 against inflation of 23.33%. However, the report warned that positive nominal returns do not necessarily translate into increased purchasing power.
Companies with pricing power, dollar-linked earnings, strong dividend capacity and hard assets were better positioned to withstand inflation. Telecommunications, consumer goods, banking and oil and gas businesses featured among the sectors with characteristics that helped protect value.
Property owners also benefited from rising replacement costs and rental income, while prospective buyers, developers and tenants faced higher acquisition, construction and financing costs.
The report described this as a widening divide between asset owners, who were better positioned to preserve wealth, and households dependent on wages or low-yield savings.
Fiscal pressures and insecurity remain major risks
Despite improvements in tax collection, Nigeria’s fiscal position remains constrained by debt servicing and a narrow revenue base.
The report cited an estimated debt-service-to-revenue ratio of 53.2% in 2025, meaning a substantial share of government revenue was absorbed by debt obligations rather than infrastructure and public services.
It also identified insecurity as a major economic risk, particularly because violence disrupts agricultural production, increases logistics costs and discourages investment. Oil theft and pipeline vandalism further weaken government revenue.
The approach of the 2027 general elections presents another risk, as political pressure could weaken the consistency of reforms that have imposed substantial costs on households and businesses.
Productivity will determine the next decade
Comercio Partners argued that Nigeria’s next phase of growth will depend on translating macroeconomic stability into higher productivity, stronger exports and better public services.
The report called for more effective public spending on power, transport infrastructure, education, healthcare, security and digital infrastructure. It also highlighted the need to expand non-oil exports and direct affordable, long-term financing towards agriculture, manufacturing, logistics and small businesses.
For households, it recommended building emergency savings, budgeting around actual living costs, setting separate savings goals and evaluating investments based on inflation-adjusted returns rather than nominal gains alone.
The report said digital financial services, regulated investment products and cooperative savings structures could help Nigerians manage economic uncertainty, but sustained progress would depend on financial discipline and consistent planning.

Family members of a 17-year-old Thai girl whose body was found in a suitcase attended a court hearing Monday
PATTAYA, Thailand -- Members of the family of a 17-year-old Thai girl whose body was discovered in a suitcase near a popular seaside resort city attended a court hearing on Monday where, for the first time, they were to see the Australian man accused of killing her.
Simon Peter Carman was arrested in June after Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) southeast of Bangkok known for tourism and its sex trade. The suitcase containing her body was found soon afterward by railway tracks in a deserted area.
Carman, who turns 46 later this month, was brought in shackles to the Pattaya Provincial Court on Monday for a procedural hearing to designate witnesses to testify.
He has been charged with murder, two counts of indecent behavior involving a minor, and concealing a corpse. A conviction on the charge of premeditated murder carries the possibility of the death penalty.
Carman had initially denied all charges, saying that he was acting in self-defense and that he did not know the girl’s real age. However, when advised by a judge on Monday that the evidence against him on hiding the victim's corpse was strong, but he could expect leniency if he confessed to that charge, he indicated that he would change his plea to guilty.
Speaking to reporters ahead of the hearing, the victim’s aunt, Miruntree Thanachai, said it would be the first time the family would meet the Australian defendant. “We previously asked the authorities, but they didn’t allow us to see him. We want to meet the person who killed our family member,” she said.
Police said the girl was last seen on security footage walking into a condominium with Carman. He was later seen leaving the building alone with a large suitcase. Security footage showed him loading it onto a motorbike and driving away.
The family said Tunchanok had gone on a vacation trip to Pattaya from their home in the rural northeastern province of Kalasin.
Carman was arrested at a Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Australia. Police said subsequent questioning led them to the suitcase with the girl’s body.
In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman said he was defending himself because the girl was threatening him with a knife.
“Simon claimed that it was self-defense, but this is not self-defense because if it is self-defense, how can my child’s teeth fall out? I want to ask,” the victim’s father, Tongchai Donhomla, told reporters. He and other family members said they had viewed the victim’s body, and that her face had been smashed in.
“I want the death penalty, but there is nothing I can do. I want the law to punish, to the fullest,” he said.
His sentiment was echoed by Miruntree Thanachai, one of the girl's aunts. “The family wants the court to sentence him to death because we have lost our family member, the important one. So we want the execution because we don’t want this to happen to others again. No one can bear this kind of damage,” she added.
On Friday, the grieving family also filed a case against Carman in civil court, asking for damages of 1.65 million baht ($49,000)

articles.title: Leading Countries in the Electronics Industry: Global Giants and Their Key Roles - وردنا
articles.summary: Leading Countries in the Electronics Industry: Global Giants and Their Key Roles  وردنا
articles.full_text:
The electronics industry is a pivotal sector driving the global economy, contributing significantly through products such as smartphones, computers, modern vehicles, communication equipment, and AI technology.
Countries hold different positions in this sector based on their roles in the supply chain; some excel in manufacturing finished products in large quantities, others in producing semiconductors and memory chips, while some focus on innovation, processor design, and manufacturing machinery used in production lines.
Which Countries Are Most Renowned for Electronics Manufacturing?
The electronics industry map features industrial powerhouses working together to produce the devices and components the world relies on daily. China leads in producing ready-made electronic devices.
Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan play crucial roles in manufacturing chips, memory, materials, and specialized equipment. The United States excels in processor design and technology development. Meanwhile, the Netherlands and Germany stand out in precision equipment and industrial electronics fields.
It's essential to differentiate between a country's share in overall electronics production and specifically in semiconductor manufacturing; each indicator has a different calculation method, and percentages cannot be directly compared without knowing the sector, period, and methodology used.
1. China: The Global Hub for Electronics Manufacturing
China plays a central role in the global electronics industry due to its large-scale manufacturing and assembly capabilities and the provision of necessary components. It boasts a vast network of factories, suppliers, and logistical service centers.
This makes it a primary production hub for smartphones, computers, screens, home appliances, and electronic equipment used across various sectors.
China leverages integrated supply chains within its industrial zones to transport components swiftly between factories before the final product is assembled and exported globally. It has a broad industrial base for producing printed circuit boards, batteries, electrical components, and smart device parts.
China's role extends beyond assembly, as it builds local capacities in chip design, manufacturing, communication technologies, and AI. However, advanced components and equipment still pose technical and industrial challenges, prompting Chinese companies to increase investment in R&D and expand domestic production.
2. Taiwan: A Global Powerhouse in Semiconductor Manufacturing
Taiwan is a crucial tech hub, particularly in manufacturing advanced semiconductors for leading smartphones, data centers, AI processors, and high-performance computing devices.
Its significance shines through with companies like TSMC, a prominent global supplier of chips for other companies, enabling specialized processor designers to turn their designs into actual chips through advanced manufacturing processes requiring extensive engineering expertise and significant investments.
Taiwan's strength lies in producing high-performance, energy-efficient chips—crucial traits for modern devices. Thus, stability in Taiwan's production is vital for global supply chains, as major disruptions could delay the production of a wide range of electronic devices.
3. South Korea: Leadership in Memory Chips and Displays
South Korea has a prominent standing in the electronics industry thanks to major companies like Samsung and SK Hynix, which play crucial roles in the semiconductor market, particularly memory chips.
DRAM memory is used in computers, phones, and servers, while NAND memory is integral to storage devices, phones, and digital gadgets. As AI applications and data centers expand, high-performance memory's importance rises to process large volumes of data quickly.
South Korea also excels at developing advanced displays, smartphones, TVs, and electronic components, combining research and development with advanced manufacturing to compete in consumer and industrial markets alike.
4. Japan: Precise Materials and High-Tech Components
Despite some consumer electronics production shifting to other Asian countries, Japan maintains a vital role in the electronics industry. Its strength lies in specialized components, high-purity chemicals, precision equipment, sensors, and components used in automotive and industrial systems.
The semiconductor industry necessitates precisely specified materials and relies on manufacturing processes with minimal error margin. Japanese companies have extensive experience in many areas, making them a critical part of supply chains even when the final product doesn’t bear a Japanese brand.
Japan also excels in automotive electronics, industrial robotics, cameras, and measurement and control devices, sustaining its standing among the world's leading technological powers.
5. United States: Processor Design and Innovation
The United States holds substantial influence in the electronics industry, not merely by the number of devices produced locally. It's a central hub for processor, GPU, and specialized chip design, alongside software, cloud platform, and AI-related technology development.
The American market is home to influential companies like Nvidia, Qualcomm, Intel, and Apple, engaged in diversified fields ranging from processors, communications, computing, and consumer electronics design.
American companies excel at investing in R&D and developing advanced designs, with some outsourced for manufacturing by specialized companies abroad.
The U.S. government is also working to enhance local chip production and mitigate risks from reliance on limited industrial hubs, reflecting the strategic importance of semiconductors for economic and industrial security and technological competitiveness.
6. Vietnam: A Growing Hub for Electronic Device Assembly
Recently, Vietnam has emerged as a key destination within electronics supply chains. Foreign investments and growth in export-oriented factories have bolstered its role in producing phones, electronics, and associated components.
The country thrives from several companies’ strategies to diversify production locations rather than relying solely on one country—an approach known as “China + 1.” It aims to distribute production risks and enhance supply chain robustness.
Global companies, including Samsung, play significant roles in Vietnam's electronics sector, benefitting from its Asian location and industrial investment capabilities. However, expanding local production of advanced components and developing engineering expertise remain vital for increasing Vietnam's added value.
7. India: Rapid Expansion in Phone and Component Manufacturing
India is eager to elevate its electronics presence by expanding smartphone production, encouraging industrial investments, and bolstering its semiconductor capabilities. Its large domestic market provides a broad demand base, attracting companies keen on scaling manufacturing operations.
India benefits from government initiatives supporting local production and investments in electronics and semiconductors. Both domestic and international companies have begun developing projects related to electronic component manufacturing, with ambitions to construct a more integrated industrial ecosystem.
Yet, reaching the level of leading advanced chip producers requires time, substantial investments, specialized expertise, and suitable infrastructure. Currently, India particularly stands out in growing phone manufacturing and device assembly while striving to expand its technical and production capabilities.
8. Malaysia: A Vital Hub for Chip Assembly and Testing
Malaysia holds a key position in the semiconductor industry, especially in chip assembly, testing, and packaging—collectively known as OSAT. These activities convert manufactured chips into usable products within electronic devices.
The country hosts specialized factories and companies in electronic components, leveraging accumulated industrial expertise and infrastructure supporting exports. These stages are essential in chip production, as the process doesn’t end with manufacturing the chip but requires testing, performance verification, and packaging per technical requirements.
With rising demand for electronic components in automotive, communications, and data center sectors, Malaysia aims to develop capabilities in higher-value activities and bolster its role within global supply chains.
9. Netherlands: Advanced Machines for Chip Manufacturing
The Netherlands holds strategic significance in the electronics industry through ASML, specialized in manufacturing photolithography systems used for semiconductor production.
EUV photolithography systems rank among the essential technologies in producing the most advanced chips, enabling semiconductor plants to execute ultra-precise patterns on silicon wafers, a crucial step in modern processor production.
Although the Netherlands doesn't primarily produce most final electronic devices, its influence stems from providing irreplaceable equipment for advanced chip manufacturing. This scenario illustrates how a country can wield significant industry power even if not ranking among the top states in assembling phones or computers.
10. Germany: Automotive Electronics and Industrial Systems
Germany stands as a key European power in industrial electronics, automotive components, control and energy systems. This reflects the German electronics sector's connection to a broad industrial base covering automotive, machinery, medical equipment, and automation systems.
Companies like Infineon play important roles in developing semiconductors used in automotive, energy, and industrial control systems. These components are gaining importance with the proliferation of electric vehicles, driver assistance systems, and technology demanding precise energy management.
Germany capitalizes on its engineering expertise, industrial quality standards, and European supplier networks.

He said its strategic location and Egypt’s free trade agreements with several countries made it attractive to industrial investors and export-oriented businesses.
He praised Thailand’s HI TECH investment, describing it as the first Thai industrial project in the zone and called for building on that experience to attract further investment across a range of industries.
