articles.title: Matrade welcomes RM60mil fund to boost MSME exports - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: Matrade welcomes RM60mil fund to boost MSME exports  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Malaysia External Trade Development Corp (Matrade) has welcomed the RM60 million allocation under the 2027 Budget to strengthen micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and expand their participation in export markets.
The fund is expected to benefit more than 3,500 companies, including 60 Bumiputera companies nationwide, including those in Sabah and Sarawak.
Matrade chairman Datuk Seri Reezal Merican Naina Merican said the allocation would reinforce confidence in the agency's role in advancing Malaysia's export agenda.
"Malaysia's double-digit export growth for the first eight months of this year reflects Malaysia's resilience amidst geopolitical uncertainties and global supply chain disruptions," he said in a statement.
He said Matrade's strategic focus was now on increasing MSMEs' participation in Malaysia's export market.
"We must elevate MSMEs as the backbone and main driver of the nation's economy, as their every success on the global stage will bring a direct spillover effect to the economic prosperity of the people," he said.
Matrade targets RM12 billion in export sales through 200 export development and promotion activities in 2027.
Malaysia's total trade reached RM2.5 trillion in the first eight months of 2026, with exports rising 31.2 per cent to RM1.36 trillion.
Matrade said it would continue implementing export strategies focusing on market diversification, halal products, services and digitalisation through the Madani Digital Trade Platform.
As of September, 10,300 MSMEs were registered with Matrade. The agency would also support MSME export development through the Matrade Academy and National Trade Blueprint.
Matrade also welcomed other budget measures supporting MSME exports, including RM1 billion in export financing by Bank Pembangunan Malaysia Bhd and an additional RM5 billion in financing by Bank Negara Malaysia to assist SMEs affected by the conflict in the Middle East.
Other measures include RM10 million for Jom Malaysia to bring rural products and high-value services to digital platforms and foreign markets, alongside RM3 billion allocated to Human Resource Development Corp for three million skills training opportunities.
Matrade said it hoped to collaborate with relevant agencies to strengthen MSME capabilities and expand exports through programmes such as eBizLink and the Matrade Academy.
It also welcomed the extension of tax incentives for international trade exhibitions until the year of assessment 2030, which is expected to encourage greater MSME participation in international trade promotion activities.

articles.title: Vietnam’s electronics import surge reflects AI demand, production expansion - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam’s electronics import surge reflects AI demand, production expansion  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s merchandise imports rose 36.7% in the first nine months of 2026, significantly outpacing export growth as electronics companies increased component inventories and expanded production capacity.
The sharp rise in imports reflects the combined impact of investment cycles, input prices and Vietnam’s growing role in global electronics supply chains, including products related to artificial intelligence.
AI boom drives imports
Vietnam’s merchandise imports reached $453.72 billion in the nine-month period, up 36.7% from a year earlier, according to the National Statistics Office. Exports totalled $434.30 billion, a year-on-year increase of 24.5%, bringing total trade to $888.02 billion, up 30.4%.
The country recorded a merchandise trade deficit of $19.42 billion over the nine-month period, although it posted a surplus of $1.27 billion in September alone.
Foreign-invested enterprises generated $350.41 billion in exports, up 29.4% year-on-year and accounting for 80.7% of the national total. By contrast, exports by domestic companies reached $83.89 billion, rising just 7.5%. The figures indicate that export growth remains heavily concentrated in the foreign-invested sector.
On the import side, foreign-invested firms recorded $335.55 billion, up 42% year-on-year, while domestic businesses imported $118.17 billion, an increase of 23.5%. The gap in growth rates suggests that import demand among foreign-invested businesses, which make up a large share of electronics and high-tech manufacturing, is expanding faster than that of domestic enterprises.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade (MoIT), machinery, equipment, raw materials and fuels used in domestic production and export processing account for around 90.5% of total imports.
Pham Van Quan, deputy director of the ministry’s Industry Agency, said the trend should also be viewed in a positive light. He said additional equipment imports could reflect efforts to expand production lines, prepare manufacturing capacity, and meet peak consumer demand at the end of the year.
Investors have assessed Vietnam’s reforms by merging localities, ministries and agencies, improving institutions and cutting administrative procedures, as moving in a positive direction, Quan said.
As a result, they have confidently scaled up production, importing additional equipment and expanding production lines in preparation for the peak consumption season in the fourth quarter. This is a peak period for manufacturing businesses, he added.
Trinh Thu Hien, deputy director of the ministry’s Agency of Foreign Trade, identified three main factors behind the increase in imports, particularly in the electronics and semiconductor sectors.
The first is rising global raw material prices. She said prices of some chips and solid-state drives (SSDs) had increased by 300% to 500%. As a result, even if import volumes remained at the previous year’s level, the value of imports could still rise sharply because of higher prices.
Second, electronics companies are increasing inventories and stockpiling raw materials to meet demand for AI-related products. Some materials have become scarce, with supply shortages occurring at times, prompting certain factories and companies to extend inventory coverage from around six weeks to 12 weeks. Meanwhile, the inventory value of some businesses has risen from $100 million to $700 million.
The third factor is production expansion by electronics and semiconductor companies. Hien cited Samsung’s increased investment in Thai Nguyen province, Intel’s relocation of a factory from Costa Rica to Vietnam, and BYD’s expansion and upgrading of its investment in Phu Tho province.
Vietnam benefits from AI supply chains, but domestic value added remains limited
The World Bank Group’s October 2026 East Asia and Pacific Economic Update said the wave of high-tech manufacturing and exports serving AI demand is supporting growth in several economies participating in global supply chains.
The WB raised its forecast for Vietnam’s GDP growth in 2026 by 1.1 percentage points from its previous projection to 7.4%. This was the largest upward revision among economies in Asia and the Pacific.
According to the report, in the 12 months ending in April 2026, six economies - China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam - exported a combined $1.4 trillion worth of AI-related goods. Over the same period, the U.S. imported around $739 billion worth of these products, with approximately one-third originating in East Asia and the Pacific.
Vietnam’s exports of AI-related goods have more than doubled compared with the 2020-2022 average. The country primarily participates in downstream equipment assembly, with computers, servers and routers accounting for around 60% of its AI-related goods exports. A significant share of these exports serves final demand in the U.S.
However, export growth has been accompanied by substantial import demand. According to the WB, Vietnam’s imports grew faster than exports in 2026, partly because companies increased their inventories of electronics, semiconductor prices rose and fuel costs remained high.
This indicates that Vietnam’s technology manufacturing and exports remain closely linked to overseas supplies of components and raw materials.
Alongside the growth opportunities, the WB also highlighted risks if expectations for AI’s economic returns are not met, potentially triggering financial market adjustments and affecting investment.
Franziska Ohnsorge, WB chief economist for Asia, said Vietnam is deeply integrated into AI-related supply chains. If the trend of strong AI demand continues, Vietnam will have significant opportunities to benefit and sustain high growth. However, this is also a risk factor because if the AI trend reverses, Vietnam’s growth could be affected.
Despite strong growth in electronics trade, domestic value added remains limited. According to the government’s assessment in Notice No. 481/TB-VPCP dated September 14, 2026, Vietnam’s electronics industry remains heavily dependent on imported components, raw materials and technology, while domestic companies have limited participation in supply chains.
Following a meeting last month with the Vietnam Electronic Industries Association and several major electronics and semiconductor import-export companies, Standing Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc instructed the Ministry of Industry and Trade to work with businesses reporting large gaps between import and export turnover, particularly those with substantial trade deficits. The aim is to clarify the structure and purpose of their imports and the extent to which these imports support production and exports.
The ministry was also tasked with reviewing the list of priority supporting-industry products for the electronics sector, focusing on components and materials with strong demand and potential for domestic production.
Another task is to develop a program to connect and develop Vietnamese suppliers for domestic and foreign electronics, semiconductor and technology firms, based on individual product supply chains, technical standards and business requirements.
At the same time, the government has called for stronger links between foreign-invested enterprises and domestic businesses, alongside support to help Vietnamese companies improve technological capabilities and quality management and participate in higher-value-added, technology-intensive stages of production.
At the MoIT’s regular press briefing, Hien, deputy director of the Agency of Foreign Trade, said the ministry’s measures focused on improving institutional and policy frameworks, developing markets and supporting businesses. In the longer term, the goal is to strengthen the capabilities of Vietnamese enterprises and increase the domestic value added of products manufactured in Vietnam.

articles.title: My Say: The SME crisis: How China’s exported over-capacity is gutting Malaysia’s private sector - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: My Say: The SME crisis: How China’s exported over-capacity is gutting Malaysia’s private sector  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
This article first appeared in Forum, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 12, 2026 - October 18, 2026
Our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are in real danger of being gutted by their hyper-competitive counterparts from China whose overcapacity is being exported to our domestic markets. They create very little domestic employment and value-add, bringing in an en bloc shipment of labour and overheads, materials and supply chain that are wholly unregulated and untaxed from China.
Malaysia’s private sector-driven SME ecosystem has almost none of the protectionist character of the monopolies and oligopolies that dominate the government-linked company (GLC)/government-linked investment company (GLIC) ecosystem. Our SMEs have to operate under strict financial discipline with limited funding liquidity, while navigating a high level of regulatory demands on their operations and high costs.
Retail units, mechanics’ workshops, construction services and supply chains, food and beverage (F&B) outlets and other service-oriented businesses are not abstract numbers on an economist’s spreadsheet. These are real enterprises that have survived for years, employed people, paid taxes and supported families and funded education for the next generation. The Chinese onslaught has already started to decimate this sector one by one. Once gone, they will never return, together with the employment of our people.
When people across such different sectors start telling the same story at the same time — margins disappearing, customers slowing down, costs rising, price competition becoming impossible and businesses simply trying to survive — we should not dismiss them as isolated business failures or a lack of ability to compete. Maybe the official macro numbers haven’t captured these yet. Maybe nobody has properly measured these or has raised the alarm. But these signals are real. By the time everyone agrees there is a crisis, a lot of these businesses will already be gone for good. Many retailers have already made it known that they will be closing shop after Chinese New Year.
We need to understand the systemic issues that the global phenomenon of China’s dominance is creating and take the necessary steps, or we shall probably see the beginning of the end for our generations-old SME sector, which is the largest tax-paying segment and the backbone of our economy.
China’s capital misallocation and the resultant exported surplus
So, let us understand why this is happening. China’s macroeconomic model today faces a persistent structural imbalance. High domestic savings rates and state-directed financial intervention have systemically prioritised industrial capacity over private consumption. China’s gross national savings rate sits at about 43% to 45% of gross domestic product (GDP), roughly double the global average.
A glaring structural problem compounds this issue: real estate historically represented 60% to 70% of Chinese household wealth. That bubble has burst, led by Evergrande and Country Garden, which together accumulated roughly US$500 billion (RM2.04 trillion) in liabilities. This problem does not seem to be going away anytime soon and the result has exacerbated several underlying issues:
● Weak consumer base: Despite generating about 30% of global manufacturing output, China’s domestic consumption remains weak.
● Capital redirection: As internal real estate investment contracts, state-backed capital has been redirected to industrial manufacturing output.
● Exporting surplus: Lacking domestic absorption capacity, state-subsidised excess production across heavy industrial goods, solar photovoltaic modules and consumer retail products are routed outwards. Today, this export push extends to the services sector.
● Growth mandates: The Chinese Communist Party’s political narrative relies heavily on economic output. GDP growth targets remain a critical key performance indicator for provincial officials.
● Scale disparity: China operates with an active workforce of 725 million people in provincial production clusters developing a hyper-competitive supply chain within these clusters. No nation on earth can match this scale or build such tightly integrated domestic supply chains.
● Provincial scale: Eleven Chinese provinces maintain working populations exceeding 30 million each — from Guangxi at around 30 million to Guangdong at around 70 million — competing fiercely in overlapping product categories.
● Global context: By comparison, the active labour forces of the European Union, the US and Brazil stand at roughly 195 million, 168 million and 108 million respectively. Malaysia’s total workforce stands at a modest 17.3 million. In short, in terms of industrial scale, there is absolutely no contest.
● Wage arbitrage realities: National Bureau of Statistics figures show that China’s urban private sector median monthly wage sits at roughly RMB4,500 (RM2,745) to RMB4,800, while its baseline rural migrant workforce averages RMB5,075. By comparison, Department of Statistics Malaysia figures place Malaysia’s formal sector median monthly wage at RM3,065. This indicates that the country’s baseline labour cost sits functionally on par with China’s, leaving Malaysian SMEs unable to rely on wage cost advantages to offset China’s massive industrial scale and state-backed capital efficiencies and subsidies.
● Urban unemployment mechanics: China’s surveyed urban unemployment rate hovers between 4.8% and 5.3%. Taking just the urban employed population of 470 million, a 5% unemployment rate represents roughly 23.5 million unemployed urban workers (excluding youth unemployment). When their unemployment number dwarfs our total workforce, and their gargantuan employed workforce has a median wage equal to or less than our own, even the most efficient businesses cannot compete with such scale.
Put together, this structural dynamic enables an unprecedented wave of global export dominance without military power, presenting an insurmountable challenge for smaller economies. Unregulated cross-border services and trade flows ensure that local providers are inevitably priced out of their own domestic market.
Global and domestic impact on Malaysian SMEs
For Malaysian SMEs, competing against this influx of capital and workforce is not merely an issue of operational efficiency. It is a matter of financial reality. Local private enterprises operate under commercial discipline, bearing standard market-rate borrowing terms and statutory tax obligations. They cannot absorb a prolonged margin squeeze against foreign entities operating under sovereign liquidity mandates that prioritise global market share over return on invested capital. They do not have the scale or almost monopolistic size to force supply chain vendors to provide practically zero-interest financing the way BYD Co, for example, does for its contractors with nearly nine-month payment terms.
This is systemic unfair trade competition that no efficiency improvement or tariffs can ever redress. I am sounding the alarm because while our consumers may enjoy lower costs now, after decades of our own economic misallocation and leakages of capital, especially within our GLIC and GLC economy, the impact will be felt when domestic SMEs disappear, and wages will be further compressed or ultimately dry up altogether along with our SMEs.
The steel sector: Enclave capital and overcapacity
The first primary industrial casualty of this dynamic we have witnessed has been Malaysia’s iron and steel sector. Malaysian Iron and Steel Industry Federation (Misif) data indicates national apparent steel consumption between 7.5 million and 9.5 million tonnes annually. However, total domestic capacity has expanded sharply past 24 million tonnes, driven primarily by mega-scale foreign investment projects.
The establishment of integrated steel complexes in the Malaysia-China Kuantan Industrial Park (MCKIP) — such as Alliance Steel (M) Sdn Bhd — introduced immense capacity into a saturated regional market:
● Capacity utilisation failure: Domestic long-steel capacity utilisation rates dropped below 50%, well beneath the 70% to 80% threshold required for cash break-even operations.
● Upstream displacements: Incumbent domestic producers such as Kinsteel Bhd and Perwaja Steel Sdn Bhd faced severe balance sheet distress, forced restructurings or liquidation. Local re-rollers operating without sovereign debt backstops could not survive below-cost market pricing.
● Enclave operations: Rather than integrating with local supply chains, these major foreign-backed industrial enclaves from China mainly import machinery, technical services and feedstock directly, minimising if not eliminating local procurement altogether. Unlike previous investment models, here multipliers and domestic wage spillovers are absent.
Across fellow Asean and BRICS economies, notably Brazil, Indonesia and Vietnam, governments have enacted anti-dumping duties and introduced strict local content mandates to preserve domestic manufacturing ecosystems. Ours provide attractive land deals and unneeded incentives, when we are already a stable political investment destination at the expense of our own domestic economy and employment.
Digital micro-retail and de minimis arbitrage
This onslaught has extended from heavy industry to light manufacturing, wholesale distribution and commercial services. The expansion of ultra-low-cost direct-from-factory e-commerce platforms bypasses traditional domestic retail networks.
While Malaysia introduced a 10% low value goods sales tax on imported goods priced below RM500, cross-border sellers continued to exploit customs tariff structures and direct-shipping subsidies. Local bricks-and-mortar retailers — bearing commercial property leases, regulatory compliance costs and standard import tariffs on bulk stock — face a structural cost disadvantage. articles.title: ASX 200 Climbs 0.7% at Midday as BHP and Copper Miners Lead Broad Rally to Start the Trading Week in Sydney - International Business Times Australia
articles.summary: ASX 200 Climbs 0.7% at Midday as BHP and Copper Miners Lead Broad Rally to Start the Trading Week in Sydney  International Business Times Australia
articles.full_text:
SYDNEY — Australian shares climbed on Monday, led by a strong rebound in mining stocks after a rally in global commodity prices, as investors returned from the weekend in a more upbeat mood following gains on Wall Street.
The benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index was up 61.1 points, or 0.70%, at 8,777.7 by midday Sydney time, extending Friday's advance.
The index had closed Friday up 0.65% at 8,716.6, ending the week on a positive note. Futures trading had pointed to a stronger start on Monday, with the SPI 200 contract signaling a gain of about 37 points before the open after a strong session in the United States.
Miners bounce back
Resources stocks did much of the heavy lifting in morning trade. The S&P/ASX 200 Materials Index rose about 1.8% by late morning, with gains spread across copper, lithium, coal and gold producers.
The rebound followed broad-based gains in commodity prices overnight, lifting mining stocks from what had been close to a 10-week low. The materials sector has been roughly flat over the past month and remains about 10% below its record high set on Aug. 25.
Mining heavyweight BHP Group rose 2.5% to 62.49 Australian dollars in early trade, giving the broader index a significant boost given its size. South32 climbed 2.6%, while Mineral Resources added 2.7%.
Copper producer Sandfire Resources was among the biggest gainers, rising 3.4%, after a rally in copper-focused stocks overseas. A U.S.-listed exchange-traded fund tracking copper miners jumped 4.3% overnight, while funds tracking gold and silver miners also posted strong gains.
Lithium stocks joined the rally, with Liontown and PLS Group each up about 3%. Steelmaker BlueScope Steel rose 3%, while coal miner Stanmore Resources gained 2.9%.
Gold miners also advanced. Northern Star Resources rose 2.1% and Capricorn Metals added 2.3%.
Technology stocks rally
Technology shares also contributed to the gains, rallying in early trade after a difficult stretch for the sector. Australian tech stocks have struggled in recent weeks as higher interest rates weighed on companies whose valuations depend on future profits.
Rates remain in focus
Despite Monday's gains, the broader backdrop for Australian equities remains challenging.
The Reserve Bank of Australia recently raised its cash rate to a 15-year high and warned it could tighten again if inflation remains stubborn. Investors are weighing whether the central bank will deliver another increase at its November meeting.
Higher borrowing costs have weighed on consumer sentiment and rate-sensitive sectors, while supporting bank profits by widening the gap between what lenders earn on loans and pay on deposits. At the same time, Australian government bond yields have climbed to multi-year highs amid a persistent global bond selloff, adding pressure on equity valuations.
Global backdrop
Sentiment was helped by Wall Street's strong finish to last week. Risk appetite had already improved on Friday after U.S. President Donald Trump pledged to halt attacks on Iran ahead of November's midterm elections, easing some concerns over geopolitical tensions and oil prices.
Still, elevated oil prices remain a concern for investors, as they feed into inflation and complicate the outlook for central banks around the world.
How the week has shaped up
Monday's gains build on a choppy period for Australian shares. The ASX 200 has spent recent weeks trading in a narrow range below the record levels it reached earlier in the year, when the index climbed above 9,000 points.
The index fell sharply on Thursday last week as miners and banks weighed, before rebounding on Friday. Gains in banks and gold stocks helped lift the market at the end of last week, offsetting weakness in major miners at that time.
With miners now joining the rally, analysts will be watching whether the momentum can continue through the afternoon session and into the rest of the week.
What to watch
Investors will be keeping an eye on commodity prices, particularly iron ore and copper, given their heavy influence on Australia's largest listed companies. Movements in global bond yields and any fresh signals from the Reserve Bank about the path of interest rates are also likely to shape market direction in the days ahead.
Corporate news is also expected to drive individual stock moves, with quarterly production updates from major miners due in the coming weeks.
The Australian market will close at 4 p.m. Sydney time.

articles.full_text:
Worth a reread, here is a new report from the front:
Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial IoT devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off – though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. In our evals, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested.
I am reminded also of those old fairy tales where the witch casts the Prince into a stone, or some other inanimate object, and he is stuck there until…?  Except this time the AI is imprisoning itself, if this were to happen in the non-test world.  Which LLM do you want in your stove?  Can you have more than one?
Told you all it was going to get weird.

articles.title: Michael Woodford, Nobel Laureate
articles.summary:
I think of Michael Woodford as the kind of economist who studies something very specific very intensively and tries to get it just right.  But in his case he is not studying something small and irrelevant, he is studying “monetary policy.” I think of him as the economist who put monetary policy and “monetarism” — […]

articles.full_text:
I think of Michael Woodford as the kind of economist who studies something very specific very intensively and tries to get it just right.  But in his case he is not studying something small and irrelevant, he is studying “monetary policy.”
I think of him as the economist who put monetary policy and “monetarism” — broadly construed — back on the map by melding it with modern theory and also modern approaches to expectations.  Think of his monetarism as for a world where interest rates and not the quantity of money are central for central bank policy.  In his world there is some nominal stickiness, and central banks can help to stabilize output without running afoul of the Lucas critique or the other problems with earlier Keynesian approaches.  He helped to enable and flesh out what macroeconomics call “the neoclassical-Keynesian synthesis” and also the New Keynesian model.  His core initial paper came in 1997 with the now-deceased Julio Rotemberg.
Expectations are critical in his model, and you can think of him as an underlying source for approaches to “forward guidance” in the world of central banking.  He also showed how a central bank could (potentially) force its way out of the zero lower bound by “irresponsibly” wishing to inflate.
It is wrong to think of Woodford as “endorsing” nominal gdp targeting, nonetheless he showed it might be optimal and overall his work has encouraged interest in that approach, much-discussed on this blog and elsewhere, most of all by Scott Sumner, a great admirer of Woodford’s.
He wrote a massive 2003 book Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy, note the title is taken from Wicksell, which I find appropriately ambitious.  His work is extremely careful and precise, and when you read it you get the feeling he has been pondering each individual question for years.
Here is Stockholm on the contributions of Woodford and Hall.  Here is Michael on scholar.google.com.  Here is Alex on Michael Woodford.

articles.full_text:
Alex has already covered this, I will add a few remarks.
First, every Bob Hall paper is interesting!  Only a handful of economists can say the same.  Every paper has an idea, and some sort of novel contribution.  His lesser-known papers can be as thought-provoking as the more famous ones.
Here is Bob on scholar.google.com.  You will notice topping the list are important papers on economic growth, even though Bob is best known for his work on the consumption function, where he gave birth to an entire literature.
One of the first Bob Hall papers I studied was his supply and demand analysis with David Lilien.  It is one of the best papers for seeing how Bob approaches every issue by thinking like an economist.
Bob also thought very creatively about how claims about the Solow residual could be translated into isomorphic claims about the gap between price and marginal cost, and for trying to apply that point to cyclical issues.  Bob is one of the best researchers for thinking about the elasticity of supply.
He did much of the core work on the Hall and Jorgensen 1967 (!) tax paper as an undergraduate.
Bob also has important papers on rent-seeking and on looting.
Second, Bob is the greatest commentator on other people’s work of all time.  He is nice and polite, but if he is assigned to your paper beware!  He will find its flaws.  He is also a famously great co-author, before that was established practice.
Third, Bob was part of the production function for Andy Hall, whose work has been covered on this blog much as of late, mostly on AI and economics/social science.  I also just learned there is a connection to Anne E. Hall at Treasury. And there is Jonathan Hall, chief economist at Amazon!
Fourth, Bob has in the past emailed me to correct typographical errors on this blog.  It is the old saying that if you want to get something done, give it to a busy person.
Here is the Nobel committee on the award, noting I find it slightly strange that they made “stabilization” the overall theme linking Bob with Michael Woodford.
An award much deserved…

articles.title: The Nobel Prize Goes to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford
articles.summary:
Twenty-five years ago Tyler told me he thought Robert Hall should win the Nobel. He has been a contender for so long today’s award was a surprise! Hall has an unusual number of unexpectedly creative papers. His best known is on consumption. Start with the textbook Keynesian model: Y = C + I + G […]
The post The Nobel Prize Goes to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Twenty-five years ago Tyler told me he thought Robert Hall should win the Nobel. He has been a contender for so long today’s award was a surprise! Hall has an unusual number of unexpectedly creative papers. His best known is on consumption.
Start with the textbook Keynesian model: Y = C + I + G + NX. Consumption is the biggest piece of Y and it also depends on Y, so C and Y have to be solved together. The consumption function was the engine of the Keynesian multiplier. The simplest version was C = a + bYd, where Yd is disposable income. Economists estimated b, forecast Y and used the forecast to predict C. Get b, the marginal propensity to consume (MPC), wrong and you get fiscal policy wrong; so a lot of work went into estimating the MPC.
Hall began instead with Milton Friedman’s permanent income hypothesis. Consumption today should depend not just on today’s income but on a consumer’s expected lifetime or permanent income. Hall added rational expectations, so people estimate their permanent income using everything they know. Many economists already accepted both ideas but Hall showed that together they imply something surprising. Consumption should follow a random walk!
Suppose you learn today that you will get a large, permanent raise starting next January. If you can save and borrow, you should start spending more today. When January’s bigger paycheck arrives, it isn’t news. You already knew it was coming.
So information that predicts your income should not predict changes in your consumption. Expected changes in income are already built into your spending plans, and only surprises cause revisions. In the simplest case (quadratic utility, free borrowing and saving, and an interest rate that just offsets impatience) the theory gives
Et(Ct+1 − Ct) = 0
Given what you know today, your best guess for the change in consumption is zero. Consumption moves only on news. Past income or any other variable shouldn’t help predict tomorrow’s consumption once you know today’s consumption.
The key point is that Hall’s test didn’t need a model of how people forecast income. The old consumption functions used things like a distributed lag on past income as a stand-in for expected future income. Hall asked a different question: does anything known today predict the change in consumption tomorrow? He found that the theory was surprisingly correct! Consumption looks like a random walk. Changes in consumption are unpredictable. Later work found consumption somewhat more predictable than Hall’s strict version allows, but the random walk became the benchmark everyone measures deviations from.
The methodological change was enormous. Instead of estimating a relationship between income and spending, economists could test restrictions implied by forward-looking choice. John Cochrane’s account of learning macroeconomics at Chicago describes how deeply Hall’s approach entered the profession’s way of thinking.
This is Hall’s most famous paper but what makes Hall interesting is the number of papers he wrote on very different topics.
Hall was part of the New Monetary Economics–Tyler with Randall Krozner wrote the book on this (alas hard to get) and see also our podcast. Hall’s contribution was a proposal for a commodity standard but not a gold or silver standard. Under a gold standard the price level moves with the relative price of gold, which swings around a lot. Hall’s alternative was to define the dollar as a fixed bundle of ammonium nitrate, copper, aluminum and plywood which he called the ANCAP standard. He chose those four because a price index of the bundle had tracked the CPI closely since the war, so pegging the dollar to the bundle would have come close to stabilizing the cost of living. He didn’t want the government stockpiling fertilizer and plywood. Private arbitrage would keep paper dollars tied to the basket. Hall offered it more as an exploration of what a commodity standard could do than as a policy he was campaigning for. Tyler has said nice things about it. And yes, ANCAP also abbreviates anarcho-capitalism. I assume that’s a coincidence.
Hall’s most famous policy idea is the flat tax, written with Alvin Rabushka at Hoover. Workers pay a single rate on wages above a generous family allowance. Businesses pay the same rate on revenue minus wages, minus purchases from other firms, minus investment, which is expensed immediately. Interest, dividends and capital gains go untaxed at the household level because the business has already paid. Add it up and you have a consumption tax, a VAT that lets workers deduct an allowance so the system keeps some progressivity. Most households could file on a postcard.
Flat tax bills appeared in Congress through the 1980s and 1990s and Steve Forbes ran on it in 1996 and 2000 but we never passed a flat tax. The idea did shape the Tax Reform Act of 1986, which cut rates and broadened the base, but the mortgage interest deduction, the charitable deduction and every other carve-out had a constituency, and the constituencies won. Public choice explains this one pretty well.
Abroad, however, the flat tax took off. Estonia went first in 1994. Russia adopted a 13 percent flat tax in 2001. Slovakia, Georgia, Romania, Bulgaria and a long list of others followed. Post-communist countries were building tax systems from scratch, without decades of entrenched deductions, and with lots of evasion that a simple low rate could reduce. Rabushka keeps the flags of about thirty countries in his Hoover office, although some later backed away.
Most of the foreign versions were flat-rate income taxes. The Hall-Rabushka plan exempted saving and investment, which makes it a consumption tax, and few countries adopted that part. Estonia came closest. It eventually stopped taxing corporate profits until they were paid out as dividends, which is the Hall-Rabushka logic applied to the business side.
Here’s one more I have cited a lot in recent years, Hall and Jones on The Value of Life and the Rise in Health Spending. Hall and Charles Jones offered a strikingly different perspective on rising health care expenditures. Most observers see health care consuming a growing share of GDP and conclude that something has gone wrong. Hall and Jones argued that it might be exactly what we should expect from growing prosperity. Here’s the simple argument. As we become richer, the marginal value of goods and services declines; another car or another vacation matters less, but another year of life becomes more valuable. Indeed, the more goods and services  you have already the more valuable another year of life becomes! It’s better to live more, the richer you are. Thus, their model suggested that it could be optimal to spend more than 30% of GDP on health care by 2050. The United States is the world’s richest large country, why shouldn’t it spend a large share of GDP on enjoying those riches for more years?

articles.title: Michael Woodford Wins Nobel
articles.summary:
No one since Milton Friedman has done more to shape how central bankers think about their jobs than Michael Woodford. Woodford’s Interest and Prices (2003) has been called the central bankers’ bible. If you have read a speech by a Fed governor in the last twenty years you have read Woodford, even if his name […]

articles.full_text:
No one since Milton Friedman has done more to shape how central bankers think about their jobs than Michael Woodford. Woodford’s Interest and Prices (2003) has been called the central bankers’ bible. If you have read a speech by a Fed governor in the last twenty years you have read Woodford, even if his name wasn’t on it.
Woodford, building on Calvo, Rotemberg, Taylor, Galí, Gertler, and others, integrated everything into a coherent, microfounded theory of monetary policy and developed its welfare implications. Households choose how much to consume using Hall’s Euler equation, firms with some market power get to change their prices only now and then, and the central bank sets the short-term interest rate. Out of these pieces comes a model in which monetary policy moves real output in the short run, and in which the main cost of inflation is that prices get out of line with one another because firms adjust at different times.
You can see the revolution since Friedman because one fun feature of Woodford’s model is that there is no money. Woodford showed you could do monetary economics in a cashless economy. That’s closer to how central banks operate today, namely, the Fed sets an interest rate and mostly ignores monetary aggregates like M2. Woodford’s book title is a homage. Interest and Prices is the English title of Knut Wicksell’s 1898 book, which argued that inflation depends on whether the central bank holds its interest rate above or below the natural rate. Woodford rebuilt Wicksell with modern tools. If Friedman taught central banks to watch the money supply, Woodford taught them to watch the gap between their policy rate and the natural rate, and to manage expectations about both.
Woodford also worked out when an interest rate rule pins down inflation. If the central bank raises nominal rates more than one-for-one with inflation, the equilibrium is determinate. If it doesn’t, expectations can become self-fulfilling (the Taylor rule but micro-founded). In a less remembered twist, he was also an early developer of the fiscal theory of the price level, which says that under some policy regimes the government’s budget determines the price level. It’s an unexpected stance for the leading New Keynesian.
